island where we send our boat on shore for water but find none they return with some Coco nut affirm that the island be very full of Coco tree which have very few nut upon they we see three or four people upon this island but they go away and will not come near we those people we imagine to be leave there to gather the and to make they ready against other shall come and fetch they the i will of bata the six and twenty we come to a anchor within a league of a great island call bata lie in twenty minute of south latitude here we build up our Shalop and name she the bat in this island be none inhabitant it do exceed abound with wood and fresh water Rivers as also with fish monkey and a kind of fowl which they affirm to be that country whereof in our time of be there I kill one which be great than a hare a great fly Squirel or bat. and in shape very like a s^^^rrill save only from each of his side do hang down two great flappe of skin which when he do leap from tree to tree he will spread forth like a pair of wing as though he do seem to fly with they they be very nimble and will leap from bough to bough oftentimes take hold with nothing but their tail because our Shalop be build in the kingdom of these beast she be call after their name the bat. the nine and twenty day travail along the shore in this island I discover a road ride under a little island about four league from i which make i very glad hope it have be our pinnace which we lose in the great storm near under the cape of Bona Esperatca with which news by night I gate aboard our general who in the morning send i with captain John davis three bark to see if we can find she but when we come to the place we find three bark ride under the island they make sign unto we to come aboard they and tell we they have hen we answer they that we will go fetch some money and will come again the next morning and buy some of they understand portuguse we dare not go aboard they because we be but evil provide the next morning be better furnish we go think to have some better commodity of they but they have weigh anchor and be all go it seem they be afraid of we by their haste away August the four of August we weigh anchor and stand for Priaman the nine of August our general man the Shalop and send we along the coast to see if we can find any roader and espy a sail we give her chase which when she perceive she can not go from we she come to a anchor and forsake their bark and row all on shore to a island in a small boat where we can not come at they we lay there bark aboard not find any one man in it the chief lade be oil nut and fine mat but see it be but such mean stuff and know that if we shall have take it our general will not have like of it we leave she not take any thing from her worth the speak of the ten and eleven day we stand close along the main land whereas we espy eight prawe ride over against a place call Tico which when we first espy we be in good hope Tico a town in sumatra that we may find our pinnace among they when we come up with they she be not there but they put we in comfort tell we there be a english ship at Priaman which be not pass six league from this town of Tico then stand out to sea we see our admiral and in short time get aboard tell our general the news we have not sail a league further their ship come on ground but our ship come on ground upon a rock of white coral but God be thank have a great gale in very short time we get she off again without any hurt at all and come near unto the road of Priaman we descry our pinnace to be there th^y meet with their pinnace which they have lose so long before Priaman in forty minute of southerly latitude which we have lose so long before in the great storm in double the cape of Bona Esperanca the captain and master of the pinnace meet we half a league from the road in their Skiffe and at our come aboard of we our general do welcome they with a peal of great ordnance and after many discourse pass of what have happen in the time of each other absence we come to a anchor in five fathom water very good ground in the road of Priaman which stand in forty minute of southerly latitude the fourteen our general send i on shore with a present to the governor and to other to see what price pepper be at and to buy fresh victual and to know whether our man may come safe on shore but when we come on shore the governor dare not speak with we private by reason of certain war that be among they by which mean they be grow jealous one of another these war grow upon this occasion the king of Achen have two son he keep the elder at home with he to succeed he after his death and the young he make king of Pedir whereupon the elder son take his father prisoner affirm that he be too old to govern any long and afterward make war upon his young brother thus see little good to be do in this place have refresh ourselves with fresh victual we resolve to depart from thence the one and twenty we weigh anchor and stand for Bantam on which day we take two prawe have nothing in they but a little rice the one of these prawe hurt two of our man very sore after they have enter she for our man think because they see some leap overboard they have all leap overboard but they be deceive for the first two man that enter be sore hurt by two which lie close hide behind their sail who assoon as they have wound they most desperate leap overboard swim away like water spaniel so take such thing as best fit we we leave their prawe do they no further harm the three and twenty we take a fisherboat have nothing of value in he let he go without any hurt save only one of they be shoot through the thigh at the first meeting when they resist we the five and twenty we descry a sail and send our Shalop longboat and Skiffe to see what she be for our ship and pinnace can not fetch she up because they be becalm these boat come up with she bid he strike sail but she will not so we fall in fight with she from three of the clock in the afternoon till ten of the clock at night by which time our pinnace have get up to we then she strike her sail and yield so we make she fast to our pinnace and tow she along with we all night in the morning our general send for they to see what they be and send three of we to see what she be lade withal when he have talk with they they tell he they be of Bantam wherefore know not what injury he may do to the english merchant a ship of Bantam take and free dismiss that have a factory in Bantam at that present and understand by we that their load be salt Rice and China dish he send they aboard their own bark again not suffer the worth of a penny to be take from they they stand towards Priaman and we towards Bantam leave each other this bark be of the burden of some forty tun the second of September we meet with a small ship of guzarate or Cambaya they take a ship of Guzarate Sillibar in four degree of southerly latitude be about eighty tun which ship we take and carry into the road of Sillibar stand in four degree of southerly latitude into which ride many prawe continual come to refresh themselves for here you may have wood water Rice buffles-flesh goat hen plant and fresh-fish but all very dear the eight and twenty day have dispatch all our business we weigh anchor and stand for Bantam the three and twenty of October we come to a anchor in the road of Marrah October the road of Marrah be in the straight of Sunda here we take in freshwater in this place be great store of buffle goat hen duck and many other good thing for refresh of man they esteem not so much of money as of Calicut clothes pintado and such like stuff the people be well use will use you well but you must look to they for steal for they think any thing well get that they can steal from a stranger the twenty eight Bantam the eight and twenty we weigh anchor and stand for Bantam which stand in six degree and forty minute of southerly latitude this day we come within three league of the town where we come to a anchor all night here we think to have see the english fleet but it be go for England three week before we come nevertheless those that remain in the country as factor of our nation come aboard we be very glad to see any of their countryman in so foreign a place and withal tell our general that the company of the hollander ship that be in the road have use very slanderous report of we to the king of Bantam the effect whereof be that we be thief and disordinate liver and such as do come for nothing but to deceive they or use such violence as time will give we leave to execute and that we dare not come into the road among they but keep two or three league from thence for fear of they after our general have hear this report it so move he that he weigh anchor send the hollander word that he will come and ride close by their side and bad the proud of they all that dare to put out a piece of ordnance upon he and withal send they word if they do go about either to brave or to disgrace he or his countryman he will either sink they or sink by their side there be of these hollander five ship the one of they of seven or eight hundred tun the rest of a far small burden but of this message notwithstanding we come and anchor close by they we never have answer but whereas the hollander be wont to swagger and keep great stir on shore all the time before our be there they be so quiet that we can scarce see one of they on land the second of November have see our countryman we take our leave and stand our course for Patane the second of November they depart from Bantam Pedra Branca three prawe and in our way as we sail between the chersonesus of malacca and Pedra Branca we meet with three prawe which be afraid of we anchor so near unto the shore that we can not come near they either with our ship or pinnace wherefore our general man his Shalop with eighteen man and send we to they to request they that for his money he may have a pilot to carry his ship to pulo Timaon which be about some five day sail from the place where we meet with they but they see our ship and pinnace at anchor about a mile from they and that they be not able to come any near they tell we plain that none of they will go with we and be at anchor weigh and be go away see that we begin a fight with they all three one of they we take in less than half a hour who man which be seventy three in all gate out of she and run on shore the other fight with we all night and in the morning about the break of day she yield unto we our general come to we in his Skiffe a little before she yield two prawe take they be lade with Benjamin storax pepper China dish and pitch the three praw get from we while we be fight with the other our general will not suffer we to take any thing from they but only two of their man to pilot we to pulo Timaon because they be of java these people of java be very resolute in a desperate case their chief weapon be javelin dart dagger and a kind of poison arrow which they shoot in trunk they have some harcubush but they be nothing expert in use they poison arrow shoot in trunk Grece a town in java they also have target the most part of they be Mahumetans they have be at Palimbam and be go back again to Greece a port town on the north-east part of java where they dwell the twelve of November we dismiss they stand our course towards Patane the six and twenty of November we see certain land bear of we northwest which neither we certain land nor our new pilot know but have a very contrary wind to stand our course for Patane we think it very necessary to search those land for wood and water hope by that time we have water to have a better wind the seven and twenty we come to a anchor within a mile of the shore in sixteen fathom good ground on the southside of these land here send our boat on shore we find some of they to be sink land nothing above the water but the tree or root of they in one of they we find a reasonable good water place and all the land a wilderness of wood it be a very uncomfortable place have neither fruit fowl nor any kind of beast wherewithal to refresh man these land we take to be some of the break land lie southeast from the i will of Bintam the break land near the i will of Bintam December the second of December have take in wood and water we weigh anchor stand our course for Patane as near as a bad wind will give we leave for we find the wind in these month to be very contrary keep still at north northwest or north-east the twelve day near unto pulo Laor we descry three sail and send our pinnace and Shalop after one of they pulo Laor be the near unto we we stay with our ship think to have meet with the other two but in the night they stand away another course so that we see they no more in the morning we descry our pinnace and Shalop about four league to leeward with the other ship which they have take the wind and current be against they another ship take they be not able to come up to we we see that go to they when we come we find she to be a juncke of pan-hange be in burden above a hundred ton lade with Rice Pan hang pepper and tin go to Bantam in java our general not esteem any such mean luggage take as much rice as serve for his provision and two little brass gun and pay they royal for all not take any thing else from they save only one man to be our pilot to Patane who be willing to come along with we when he see our general use they so well the other two pilot which we take before out of one of the three prawe be unskilful man wherefore our general reward they for the time that they have be with he send they back again into their own country by the juncke which we take that be go to java the thirteen day we leave she stand our course for pulo Timaon pulo Timaon over against pan-hange join on the king of pan-hange his country here we be trouble very much with contrary wind and current for the sea run always from the begin of November to the begin of April to the southward and from April to November back again to the northward the wind also in the aforesaid first five month be most common northerly the monsons in these part and in the other seven month southerly all the ship of China Patane jor pan-hange and other place which be to the northward come to Bantam or Palimbam when the northerly be come and return back again when the southerly come which monsoin come in the month before mention this be observe you shall have both wind and tide with you here as I say before I find such contrary violent wind and current in three week he can not get one league a head that I can not in three week get a league a head this country of pan-hange be a very plentiful country and full of gentry after the fashion of those country store of ship and victual very cheap this country lie between jor and Patane and reach on the sea-coast to cape Tingeron be a very high cape and the first land-fall that the carack of Macao or junck of China cape Tingeron or Camboia prawe do make as they come for malacca java sumatra jumbe jor Palimbam Grece or any other part to the southward here as I stand for patane about the twenty seven of December I meet with a juncke of the japon which have be pyrate along the coast of China and Camboia their pilot be dead with ignorance and foul weather they have cast away their ship on the shold of the great island borneo and to enter into the country of borneo they dare not for the japon be not suffer to land in any port in India with weapon be account a people so desperate and dare that they be fear in all place where they come these people their ship be split with their shalop enter this juncke wherein I meet they which be of Patane and kill all the people sa^e one old pilot. this juncke be lade with Rice which when they have possess and furnish with such furniture necessary and arm as they save out of their sink ship they shape their course for japan b^t the badness of their juncke contrary wind and unseasonableness of the year force they to leeward which be the cause of my unlucky meet they after I have hale they and make they come to lee-ward send my boat aboard they I find they by their man and furniture very unproportionable for such a ship as they be in which be a juncke not above seventy ton in burden and they be ninety man and most of they in too gallant a habit for sailor and such a equality of behaviour among they that they seem all fellow yet one among they there be that they call captain but give he little respect I cause they to come to a anchor and upon further examination I find their lade to be only rice and for the most part spill with wet for their ship be leak both under and above water upon question with they I understand they to be man of war that have pillage on the coast of China and Camboia and as I say before have cast away their ship on the shold of borneo here we ride at anchor under a small island near to the i will of Bintam two day entertain they with good usage not take any thing from they think to have gather by their knowledge the place and passage of certain ship on the coast of China to have make my voyage but these rogue be desperate in wind and fortune being hopeless in that paltry juncke ever to return to their country resolve with themselves either to gain my ship or to lose their life and upon mut^all courtesy with gift and feast between we sometime fi^e and twenty or six and twenty of their chief come aboard whereof I will not suffer above six to have weapon their be never the like number of our man aboard their juncke I will captain John davis in the morning to possess himself of their weapon and to put the company before mast and to leave some guard on their weapon while they search in the rice doubt that by search and find that which will dislike they they may sudden set upon my man and put they to the sword as the sequel prove captain davis be beguile with their humble semblance will not possess himself of their weapon though I send twice of purpose from my ship to will he to do it they pass all the day my man search in the rice and they look on at the sunne-setting after long search and nothing find save a little storax and Benjamin they see opportunity and talk to the rest of their company which be in my ship be near to their juncke they resolve at a watchword between they to set upon we resolute in both ship this be conclude they sudden kill and drive overboard all my man that be in their ship and those which be aboard my ship sally out of my cabin where they be put with such weapon as they have find certain target in my cabin and other thing that they use as weapon myself be aloft on the deck know what be likely to follow leap into the waste where with the boat swain carpenter and some few more we keep they under the halfe-decke at their first come forth of the cabin they meet captain davis come out of the gun-roome captain John davis slay who they pull into the cabin and give he six or seven mortal wound they thrust he out of the cabin before they his wound be so mortal that he die assoon as he come into the waste they press so fierce to come to we as we receive they on our pike they will gather on our pike with their hand to reach we with their sword it be near half a hour before we can stone they back into the cabin three or four of the japonian leader kill in which time we have kill three or four of their leader after they be drive into the cabin they fight with we at the least four hour before we can suppress they often fire the cabin burn the bedding and much other stuff that be there and have we not with two demy-culuering from under the halfe-decke beat down the bulk head and the pump of the ship we can not have suppress they from burn the ship this ordnance be charge with crosse-barre bullet and case-shot and bend close to the bulk head so violent mar therewith board and splinter one and twenty japoan slay with demiculuer shoot that it leave but one of they stand of two and twenty their leg arm and body be so tear as it be strange to see how the shot have massacre they in all this conflict they never will desire their life though they be hopeless to escape such be the desperateness of these japonian only one leap overboard which afterward swim to our ship again and ask for grace we take he in and ask he what be their purpose he tell we that they mean to take our ship and to cut all our throat he will say no more but desire that he may be cut in piece the next day to wit the eight and twenty of December we go to a little island to the leeward of we and when we be about five mile from the land the general command his people to hang this japonian but he break the rope and fall into the Sea I can tell whether he swim to the land or not we take our course right to the little foresaid island and come there to a anchor the thirty of December we remain there three day to mend our boat and to take in wood and water in this island we find a ship of Patane out of which we take the captain and ask he whether the ship of China be come to Patane or no he tell we that they be not yet come but that they will come thither within few day we make the captain of that ship to be our pilot because he know very well to what place the chinish ship will come the ten of january we purpose to stay their till it please God that we shall meet the chinish ship the twelve of januarie one of our mate climb up to the top of the mast and descry two ship which come towards we but because of the wind they be force to go to the lee-ward of the island assoon as we have sight of they we weigh anchor and make towards they and we fetch up the great of they the twelve of januarie in the night we fight a little with they and board they and bring they to a anchor the next day to wit the thirty of januarie we unlade some of their good to wit raw silk and other silk they have fifty ton of silver of their country but we take little or none of it because we have good hope that we shall meet with the other chinish ship after we have take some of their silk we let they depart the fifteen of january and give they twice as much as we have take from they and cast they off we take our course back again to China bata they return from the i will of Bintam two small land call pulo sumatra but we can not fetch it up because we have contrary wind so that we be force to put lee-ward unto two small land which they of java call pulo sumatra where we come to a anchor the two and twenty of januarie the four and twenty day as we ride at anchor there arise a great storm of wind with which our cable break so that we be force to put into the near creek the second of February five Holland ship meet with we sail homeward which put into the same road where we be February captain Warwick be general of these ship he send to our general to dine with he our general go to he he tell we that our english merchant in Bantam be in great peril and that still they look for nothing else then that the king of java will assault they because we have take the china ship whereby the king of Bantam have lose his custom wherefore captain Warwick request our general that he will cease to go any further and will sail home unto England with he our general answer that he have not as yet make his voyage and that therefore he will not return until it shall please God to send he somewhat to make up the game the hollander perceive that they can not persuade our general to give over his purpose February the three depart from we the three of February our general consider that if he shall proceed on his voyage it will be very dangerous for the english merchant which be resident in those part and see that he have but two anchor and two cable to help himself withal think good to repair his ship and to return home with that poor voyage that he have make when our ship be ready and that we have take in wood and water they return home we hoist up our sail the five of February to return for England the seven of April we have sight of the cape of Bona esperanza after we have pass a great storm April 7. 1606. the seventeen of April we come to the i will of Helena where we water Helena and find refreshment as wine and goat which we ourselves kill in the say island be many wild swine and goat there be also great store of partridge Turkey cock and guinea hen this island be not inhabit we depart from thence the three of may. the fourteen we pass under the equinoctial line may. they arrive in Milford haven in Wales they come to Portsmouth the seven and twenty of june we arrive in Milford haven in Wales the nine of july we come to a anchor in Portsmouth roade where all our company be dismiss and here we advancement of trade of merchandise within our say realm and the dominion of the same may adventure may set forth one or more voyage with convenient number of ship and Pynnasses by way of traffic and therefore that we great tender the honour of our nation the wealth of our people and the encouragement of they and other of our love subject in their good enterprise for the increase of our navigation HUBERD chap. 3 the first voyage make to east India by master JAMES lancaster now knight for the merchant of London 1600. with four tall ship to wit the dragon the Hector the ascension and Susan and a victualler call the guest @ i. the preparation to this voyage and what befall they in the way till they depart from Saldania the merchant of London in the year of our lord 1600. join together and make a stock of seventy two thousand pound to be employ in ship and merchandize for the discovery of a trade in the east India to bring into this realm spice and other commodity they buy four great ship to be employ in this voyage the dragon of the burden of six hundred ton the Hector of the burden of three hundred ton the Ascentic^ of the burden of two hundred and threescore ton these ship they furnish with man victual and munition for twenty month and send in they in merchandise and spanish money to the value of seven and twenty thousand pound all the rest of their stock be spend and consume about the ship and other necessary appertain to they with money lend to the mariner and sailor beforehand that go upon the voyage the merchant be suitor to her majesty who give they her friendly letter of commendation write to diverse prince of India offer to enter into a league of peace and amity with they the copy of which letter shall hereafter appear in their place and because no great action can well be carry and accomplish without a absolute authority of justice shee grant to the general of their fleet master james Lancaster for his better command and government a commission of marshal Law the thirteen of February 1600. the say master james Lancaster the general be place in the dragon the great ship be admiral master John Middleton captain in the Hector the vide-admiral master William Brand chief governor in the ascension and master John Heyward in the Susan and more in every of the say ship three merchant to succeed one the other if any of they shall be take away by death these ship be ready and depart from Wolwich in the river of Thames the thirteen of February after the english account 1600. with four hundred and fourscore man in they in the dragon two hundred and two man in the Hector a hundred a eight in the ascension fourscore and two and in the Susan fourscore and eight the guest a ship of a hundred and thirty ton be add as a victualler these ship stay so long in the river of Thames and in the down for want of wind that it be Easter day before they arrive at Dartmouth where they spend five or six day in take in their bread and certain other provision appoint for they from thence they depart the eighteen of April 1601. and ride in Tor bay till the twenty in the morning while we ride there the general send aboard all the ship instruction for their better company keep at their come to the sea and further give direction if any of the fleet shall be separate the one from the other by storm of wind tempest or other casualty what * * April 1601. these place be the calm of Canary and if weakness permit not to double the cape So^danha the three cape saint Roman in Madagascar to cirne and so to Suma^ra their first place of trade may the five place to repair unto for their meeting together again the second of April 1601. the wind come fair and we hoist our anchor and depart out of Tor bay direct our course towards the land of the canaria the wind hold fair the five of May in the morning we have sight of Alegranza the northermost island of the Canarias and direct our course between Forteventura and the grand canaria and come to the south part of the grand canaria think to water there we fall into the calm which proceed by reason of the high-land that lie so near the seaside the seven of May about three of the clock in the afternoon we depart from the grand canaria have the wind at north-east and we direct our course south-west by south and south south-west till we come into 21. 1 degree from the eleven to the twenty our course be for the most part south till we come into eight degree the wind be always northerly and north-east in this height we find the calm and contrary wind which upon this coast of Guinea at this time of the year be very familiar with many sudden gust of wind storm thunder and lightning very fearful to be see and dangerous to the ship unless a diligent care be have that all sail be strike down upon the sudden perceive the air never so little to change or alter and yet many time although the master of ship be careful and look unto it with great diligence the suddenness be such that it can hardly be prevent from the twenty of May till the one and twenty of june we lay the most part becalm and with contrary wind at south and turn up and down with this contrary wind with much ado^ we get into two degree of the north side of the line where we espy a ship to the which the general give chase command all the rest of the ship to follow he and by two of the clock in the afternoon we have set she up and take she she be of the city of viana in Portugal and come from Lisbon in the company of two carracke and three galleon find for the east India which ship she have lose at Sea the three galleon be ship of war and go to keep the coast of the east India from be trade with other nation we take out of her a hundred six and forty butt of wine a hundred threescore and sixteen jar of oil twelve barrel of oil and five and fifty hogshead and fat of meal which be a great help to we in the whole voyage after the general divide these victual indifferent to all the ship to every one his proportion without partiality the last of june about midnight we double the line and lose the sight of the north-star have the wind at southeast and we hold our course south south-west and double the cape of saint Augustine some six and twenty league to the eastward the twenty of july we be shoot into nineteen degree forty minute to the southward of the line the wind inlarge daily to the eastward here we discharge the guest the ship that go a long with we to carry the provision that our four ship can not take in in England after we have discharge she we take her mast sail and yards and break down her high building for firewood and so leave she float in the sea and follow our course to the southward the four and twenty of july we pass the tropic of Capricorn the wind be north-east by north we hold our course east southeast now by reason of our long be under the line which proceed of our late come out of England for the time of the year be too far spend by six or seven week to make a quick navigation many of our man fall sick therefore the nine and twenty of july be in 28.1/^ degree he write a remembrance to the governor of each ship either to fetch Saldavia or saint Helena for refresh thus follow on our course the first of August we come into the height of thirty degree August south of the line at which time we meet the south-west wind to the great comfort of all our people for by this time very many of our man be fall sick of the scurvy in all our ship and unless it be in the general ship only the other three be so weak of man that they can hardly handle the sail this wind hold fair till we come within two hundred and fifty league of the cape esperanza and then come clean contrary against we to the east and so hold some fifteen or sixteen day to the great discomfort of our man for now the few whole man we have begin also to fall sick so that our weakness of man be so great that in some of the ship the merchant take their turn at the helm and go into the top to take in the top-sail as the common mariner do but God who show mercy in all distress send we a fair wind again so that the nine of September we come to Saldania where the general before the rest bear in and come to a anchor they arrive at S^ldania and hoist out his boat to help the rest of the ship for now the state of the other three be such that they be hardly able to let fall a anchor to save themselves withal the general go aboard of they and carry good store of man and hoist out their boat for they which they be not able to do of themselves and the reason why the general man stand better in health then the man of other ship be this he bring to sea with he certain bottle of the juice of lemon the best remedy for the scurvy which he give to each one as long as it will last three spoonful every morning fast not suffer they to eat any thing after it till noon this juice work much the better if the party keep a short diet and whole refrain salt meat which salt meat and long be at the sea be the only cause of the breed of this disease by this mean the general cure many of his man and preserve the rest so that in his ship have the double of man that be in the rest of the ship he have not so many sick nor lose so many man as they do which be the mercy of God to we all after the general have holpen the rest of the ship to hoist out their boat they begin all to be great comfort then he himself go present aland to seek some refresh for our sick and weak man where he meet with certain of the country people and give they diverse trifle as knife and piece of old iron and such like the most universal language and make sign to they to bring he down sheep and oxen. for he speak to they in the cattle language which be never change at the confusion of Babel which be moth for ox and kine and baa for sheep which language the people understand very well without any interpreter after he have send the people away very well content with their present and kind usage order be present give that certain of every ship company shall bring their sail aland and build tent with they for their sick man and also to make fortification of defence defence necessary if by any occasion the people shall take any conceit of offence against we and thereby offer we any violence and the general prescribe a order for buy and s^lling with the people which be manner of trade with the savage that at such time as they shall come down with the cattle only five or six man appoint for that purpose shall go to deal with they and the rest which shall never be under thirty musket and pike shall not come near the market by eight or ten score at the near and always to stand in their rank in a readiness with their musket in their rest what occasion soever shall befall and this order be most strict observe and keep that no man dare once go to speak with any of the people without special leave and I take this to be the cause why we live in so great friendship and amity with they contrary to that which late have befall the hollander which have five or six of their man slay by their treachery the three day after our come into this bay of Saldania the people bring down beef and mutton which we buy of they for piece of old iron hoop as two piece of eight inch a piece for a ox and one piece of eight inch for a sheep with which they seem to be well content within ten or twelve day we buy of they a thousand sheep and two and forty ox and may have buy many more if we will now within twelve day they cease to bring we any more cattle but the people many time come down to we afterward and when we make they sign for more sheep they will point we to those we have buy which the general cause to be keep graze upon the hill about our tent and be the cause as we judge they think we will have inhabit there and therefore bring we no more but God be thank we be well store to satisfy our need and may then very well forbear buy these ox be full as big as we and be very fat and the sheep many of they much big but of a very hairy wool yet of exceed good flesh fat and sweet this bay be in 34. degree south of the line and to our think much better than our sheep in England the people of this place be all of a tawny * * quality of the people and their difficult language the healthfulness of this Bay colour of a reasonable statute swift of foot and much give to pick and steal their speech be whole utter through the throat and they clock with their tongue in such sort that in seven week which we remain here in this place the sharp wit among we can not learn one word of their language and yet the people will soon understand any sign we make to they while we stay here in this bay we have so royal refresh that all our man recover their health and strength only four or five except but before our come in and in this place we lose out of all our ship one hundred and five man and yet we make account we be strong at our departure out of this bay than we be at our come out of England our man be so well enure to the southern climate @. 2 their departure from Saldania and proceed in their voyage to Achen in sumatra with their trade at saint Maries Antongill Nicubar the refresh one may very well refresh there over the bay of Saldania stand a very high hill flat like a table and be call the table such another plain mark to find a harbour in be not in all that coast Sunday the first of November in the morning we double the cape of have the wind west north-west a great gale the six and twenty of November we fall with the head-land of the island of saint Laurence somewhat to the east of cape Sebastian and be within five mile of the shore we sound and find twenty five fathom the variation of the compass be little more or less sixteen degree for in a east and west course the variation of the compass help much and especial in this voyage decemb. 15. from the six and twenty of November till the fifteen of December we ply to the eastward the near our course we can lie always strive to have get to the island of Cirne i will of Cirne or d. Rodrigues which in some card be call Diego Rodriques but we find the wind always after our come to the island of saint Laurence at east and east southeast and east north-east so that we can not obtain it and to strive long in hope of change of wind we can not for now our man begin again to fall sick of the scurvy then the captain of the vice-admiral call to the general and think it best to bear into the bay of Antongile and there to refresh our man with orange and lemon to clear ourselves of this disease which be by he and the whole counsel call for that purpose well approve the seventeen of December we have sight of the southermost part of the island of saint Mary isle of s. Mary and s. Laurence and the next day we anchor between saint Mary and the great island of saint Laurence and send our boat aland to saint Maries where we have some store of lemon and orange which be precious for our diseased man to purge their body of the scurvy now as we ride here buy orange end lemon there arise upon we a very great storm so that three of our ship be put from their Anchros but within some sixteen hour the storm cease and the ship return and weigh their anchor again the general think it not good to make any long stay there see the uncertainty of the weather and that there be upon this island so little refresh to be have only these orange and lemon a little goat milk and some small quantity of Rice we see only one cow and that they drive away assoon as they see we come on land see this place so dangerous to ride in the general give present order to sail towards the bay of Antongile the time of the year be spend the easterly wind come against we and our man sick people of s. mar^e this island of s. Mary be high land and full of wood the people be black very handsome and tall man and of curl hair only before in their forehead they strike it up as the woman do here in England so that it stand some three inch upright they be whole without apparel only their privy part cover they be very tractable to converse withal yet seem to be very valiant the most of their food be Rice and some fish yet at our be there we can buy but small store of rice for the time of their store be far spend and their harvest be at hand there be two or three water place on the north part of this island but none of they very commodious yet with some travel there be water enough to be have the twenty three of December we depart from this island of s. Mary and the twenty five be Christmas day we come into the bay of Antongill decemb. 23. the bay of Antongill and come to a anchor in eight fathom water between a small island and the main lie in the bottom of the bay a very good and a safe road but the best ride be near under a small island for the defence of the wind that blow there for while we abide in this bay there blow a exceed great storm and those of our ship that ride near the small island be under the wind speed best for two of our ship drive with three anchor ahead the ground be ozy and not firm at our go a land in the little island we perceive by write upon the rock of five Holland ship which have be there and be depart about two month before our come in and have have some sickness among their man and have lose as we perceive between one hundred and fifty and two hundred man while they ride in that place the next day after our come to a anchor we go a land to the main island where the people present repair to we and make we sign of the five Holland ship depart and that they have buy the most part of their provision yet they enter into barter with we for Rice and hen orange and lemon and another fruit call and hold all at high rate and bring but a pedlar quantity our market be near to a great river into which we go with our boat and some man that be appoint to be buyer go ashore the rest remain in the boat always ready with their weapon in their hand and the boat some fifteen or twenty yard off into the water where the people can not wade to they and be ready at all time if they a shore have have any need to take they in so we trifle off some day before as aforesaid we can bring they to any real trade for all these people of the south and east part be very subtle and crafty in their barter buy and sell that unless you hold a near hand with they you shall hardly bring they to trade in any plain sort for they will ^ift you continual to give a little more and t^en no man will sell without that price so that you must not enlarge to any one more than another for in so do the want of this discretion in Virginia while one out of need or seem bounty will give a great price than another to the savages for their comedy so heigthn the prize and make they overvalue their corn etc that it prove much hindrance to the plantation a pinnace rear all will have that price or none the general see this command measure to be make of almost a quart and appoint how many glass bead shall be give for every measure and he that will not deal in this manner shall not deal at all the like order be set down for orange lemon and how many for every bead or else not our merchant after a little hold off consent and our deal be frank and round without any contradiction or word so that while we abide here we bring 15. @ ton of rice forty or fifty bushel of their pease and bean great store of orange lemon and and eight beef with many hen while we ride in this bay we rear a pinnace which we bring in piece in our ship out of England and cut down tree of which there be very great and great store which tree we saw out in board and sheathe she this pinnace be of some eighteen ton and very necessary and fit to go before our ship at our come into India in the time we stay here there die out of the general ship the master mate the preacher and the surgeon with some ten other common man and out of the vice-admiral there die the master with some other two and out of the ascension by a very great mischance be slay the captain and the boatswaine mate for as the master mate out of the general ship be carry a land to be bury the captain of the ascension take his boat to go aland to his burial and as it be the order of the sea to shoot off certain piece of ordnance at the burial of any officer the gunner of the ordnance shoot off three piece and the bullet be in they one stroke the ascension boat and slay the captain and the boatswaine mate stark dead how vain a thing be man so that they that go to see the burial of another be both bury there themselves those that die here die most of the flux which in our opinion come with the water which we drink for it be the time of winter when it rain very much which cause great flood to overflow the country so that the water be not wholesome as in most place in these hot country they be not in the time of their reins this disease also of the flux be often take by go open and cold in the stomach which our man will often do when they be hot we set sail out of this bay the six of march an^ h^ld on our course towards the India and the sixteenth we fall with a island call rogue-pize which lie in 10. ^/^ degree to the south of the equinoctial line to this island the general send his boat the isle of rogue-pize to see whether there be any safe ride for the ship but the boat for the most part find deep water where the ship can not safe ride as we coast along this island it seem very fair and pleasant exceed full of foul and Coco nut-tree and there come from the land such a pleasant smell as if it have be a garden of flower and sure if there be any good ride for ship in this island it must needs be a place of very great refresh for as our boat go near the land they see great store of fish and the fowl come wonder about they in such sort that with the oar wherewith the mariner rowe^ they kill many which be the fat and the best that we taste all the voyage and of these there be such exceed great abundance that many more ship than we have with we may have refresh themselves therewith 1602. dangerous rock the thirty of march 1602. be in six degree to the south of the line we happen upon a ledge of rock and look overboard and see they under the ship about five fathom deep it much amaze we fall upon the sudden and unexpected then as we be present cast about the ship we find eight fathom and so hold on our course east one of our man be in the top see a island southeast of we some five or six league off be but low land thisle of Candu this we judge to be the island of Candu although in our course we can not by computation find ourselves so far shoot to the eastward bear on our course some thirteen or fourteen league other rock we fall upon another flat of rock then we cast about to the southward and sail some twelve league find other rock so that prove diverse way we find flat of rock round about we and twenty and thirty and in some place forty and fifty fathom water in the midst of the flat here we be for two day and a half in exceed danger and can find no way to get out but at last we resolve to seek to the northward and in six degree forty three minute God be thank we find six fathom water the pinnace always go before we and sound with commandment to make sign what depth she have that thereby we may follow she thus thanks be to God be deliver out of this pound we follow our course with variable wind till the nine of May about four of the clock in the afternoon the isle of Nicubar at which time we have sight of the land of Nicubar and bare in and anchor on the north-side of the channel but the wind change to the south-west we be force to hoist our anchor and to bear over to the southside of the channel and so come to a anchor under a small island that lie on the say shore here we have fresh water and some Coco nut other refresh we have little yet the people come aboard our ship in long canoas which will hold twenty man and above in one of they and bring gum to sell in stead of amber and therewithal deceive diverse of our man for these people of the east be whole give to deceit they bring also hen and Coco nut to sell but hold they very dear so that we buy few of they we stay here ten day place of our ordnance and trim of our ship because we will be in all readiness at our arrival at our first port which we be not now far from April 20. the twenty of April in the morning we set sail to go towards sumatra but the wind blow so hard at south south west and the currant be against we that we can not proceed but beat up and down our ship fall into two leak so that we be force to go to the island of Sombrero the i will of Sombrero some ten or twelve league to the northward of Nicobar here we in the admiral lose a anchor for the ground be foul and grow full of counterfeit coral and some rock which cut our cable asunder so that we can not recover our anchor the people of these land go naked have only the privity find up in a piece of linen cloth which come about their middle like a girdle and so between their twist they be all of a tawny colour and anoint their face with diverse colour they be well limbed but very fearful for none of they will come aboard our ship or enter into our boates. the general report that he have see some of their priest or sacrificer all apparel but close to their body as if they have be sew in it and upon their head a pair of horn turn backward with their face paint green black and yellow and their horn also paint with the same colour and behind they upon their buttock a tail hang down very much like the manner as in some paint clothes we paint the devil in our country he demand wherefore they go in that attire answer be make he that in such form the devil appear to they in their sacrifice and therefore the priest his servant be so apparel tree sufficient for main mast a strange plant. in this island grow tree which for their tallness greatness and straightness will serve the big ship in all our fleet for a main mast and this island be full of those tree here likewise we find upon the sand by the sea side a small twig grow up to a young tree and offer to pluck up the same it shruke down into the ground and sink unless you hold very hard and be pluck up a great worm be the root of it and look how the tree grow in greatness the worm diminish now as soon as the worm be whole turn into the tree it root in the ground and so grow to be great this transformation be one of the strange wonder that I see in all my travail for this tree be pluck up little the leave strip off and the pill by that time it be dry turn into a hard stone much like to white coral so that this worm be twice transform into different nature of these we gather and bring home many @. 3 their entertainment and trade at Achen 29. of may. 1602. sumatra the nine and twenty of May we set sail from this island of Sombrero and the second of june we have sight of the land of sumatra and the five of june we come to anchor in the road of Achen some two mile of the city where we find sixteen or eighteen sail of ship of diverse nation some goserats some of Bengala some of Calicut call Malabares some pegues and some patanye which come to trade there there come aboard of we two holland merchant which have be leave there behind their ship to learn the language and manner of the country these tell we we shall be very welcome to the king who be desirous to entertain stranger and that the queen of England be very famous in those part by reason of the war and great victory the fame of q. Elizabeth which she have get against the king of Spain the same day the general send captain John Middleton captain of the vide-admiral with four or five gentleman to attend upon he to the king to declare unto he that he be send from the general of those ship who have a message and a letter from the most famous queen of England to the most worthy king of Achen and sumatra and that it will please his royal majesty to give to the say messenger audience to deliver his message and letter with a sufficient warrant for the safety of he and his people according to the law of nation hold in that behalf this messenger be very kind entertain by the king who when he have deliver his message glad grant his request and commune with he about many question and after cause a royal banquet to be make he and at his departure give a robe and a tuck of calico wrought with gold which be the manner of the king of this place to those he will grace with his special favour and withal send his commendation to the general will he to stay one day aboard his ship to rest himself after his come from the disquiet sea and the next day to come a land and have kind audience and frank leave with as great assurance as if he be in the kingdom of the queen his mistress and if he doubt of any thing of this his royal word such honourable pledge shall be send he for his further assurance as he shall rest very well satisfy therewith the three day the general go a land very well accompany with some thirty man or more to attend upon he and first at his land the holland merchant meet he and carry he home to their house as it be appoint for as yet the general will make choice of no house of his own till he have speak with the king but stay at the hollander house till a noble man come from the king who salute the general very kind and declare that he come from his majesty and represent his person then he demand the queen letter of the general which he refuse to deliver say he will deliver it to the king himself for it be the order of ambassador in those part of the world from whence he come to deliver their letter to the prince own hand and not to any that do represent the king person so he demand to see the superscription which the general show he and he read the same and look very earnest upon the seal take a note of the superscription and do likewise write her majesty name and then with courtesy take his leave and repair to the court to tell the king what have pass who present send six great elephant the honourable entertainment of the english general by the king of Achen with many trumpet drum and streamer with much people to accompany the general to the court so that the press be exceed great the big of these elephant be about thirteen or fourteen foot high which have a small castle like a coach upon his back cover with crimson velvet in the middle thereof be a great basin of gold and a piece of silk exceed rich wrought to cover it under which her majesty letter be put the general be mount upon another of the elephant some of his attendant ride other go a foot but when he come to the court gate there a noble man stay the general till he have go in to know the king further pleasure but present the say nobleman return and will the general to enter in and when the general come to the king presence he make his obeisance after the manner of the country declare that he be send from the most mighty queen of England to congratulate with his highness and treat with he concern a peace and amity with his majesty if it please he to entertain the same and therewithal begin to enter into further discourse which the king break off say I be sure you be weary of the long travail you have take I will have you to sit down and refresh yourself you be very welcome and here you shall have whatsoever you will in any reasonable condition demand for your princess sake for she be worthy of all kindness and frank condition be a princess of great nobleness for fame speak so much of she the general perceive the king mind deliver he the queen letter which he willing receive and deliver the same to a noble man stand by he then the general proceed to deliver he his present which be a basin of silver with a fountain in the midst of it weigh two hundred and five ounce a great stand cup of silver a rich lookingglass a head-piece with a plume of feather a case his divine knowledge and providence have so dispose his blessing and good thing of his creation for the use and nourishment of mankind in such sort that notwithstanding they grow in diverse kingdom it shake all the iron work of she Rother and the next day in the morning our Rother break clean from the stern of our ship and present sink into the Sea they lose their Rother in a storm this strike a present fear into the heart of all man so that the best of we and most experience know not what to do and special see ourselves in such a tempestuous sea and so stormy a place so that I think there be few worse in all the World now our ship drive up and down in the sea like a wrack which way soever the wind carry she so that sometime we be within three or four league of the cape esperanza then come a contrary wind almost 40. degree o^ south latitude and drive we almost to forty degree to the southward into the hail and snow and sleet cold weather and this be another great misery unto we that pinch we exceed sore so that our case be miserable and very desperate yet all this while the Hector keep by we careful the company whereof be some comfort unto we and many time the master of the Hector come aboard our ship so at the the last it be conclude to take our mizzen mast and put it forth at the stern port to prove if we can steer our ship into some place where we may make another Rother to hang it to serve our turn home but this device be to small purpose for when we have fit it and put it forth the sea be somewhat grow with lift up the mast it do so shake the stern and put all in such danger that it be needful to make all convenient haste to get the mast into the ship again which we be very glad when we have bring it to pass now we be without all remedy unless we make a new Rother and can bring it to pass to hang it in the sea which to perform let every man judge how easy a thing it be our ship be of seven or eight hundred t^nnes and in so dangerous a sea as this be but necessity compel to prove all mean then the general command the carpenter to make a Rother of the say mizzen mast to prove what we can do but this bar fall in our way that at such time as we lose anchor for the which thank be almighty God who have deliver we from infinite peril and danger in this long and tedious navigation chap. 4 a discourse of java and of the first English factory there with diverse indian english and dutch occurrent write by master EDMUND scot contain a history of thing do from the eleven of February 1602. till the six of October 1605. abbreviated @. i. the description of with the manner and fashion of the people both javan and chynaess which do there inhabit be a island which lie in a hundred and forty degree of longitude from the middle part of it and the inhabitant and in the nine degree of latitude be also about a hundred forty and six league long east and west and some ninety league broad south and north the middle part of which land be for the most part all mountain the which be not so steep but that people do travel to the top of they both on horseback and on foot some inhabitant do dwell upon those hill which stand next to the sea but in the very middle of the land so far as ever I can learn the mid. land there be no inhabitant but there be wild beast of diverse sort whereof some do repair near the valley adjoin to the sea and devour many people towards the sea for the most part be low moorish ground wherein stand their principal town of trade the chief whereof lie on the north and north-east side of the island as chiringin Bantam jackatra and i^rtan or Greesey the city the which low ground be very unwholesome and breed many disease especial unto stranger which come thither and yield no merchandise worthy trade for or speak of but pepper the which have be bring in time pass from all place of the land to Bantam as the chief mart town of the county which town for trade do far exceed Achen or any town or city thereabouts and pepper be wont to be bring thither from diverse other country which of late year be not by reason that the dutchman trade to every place and buy it up this town of Bantam be about three english mile in length also very populous there be three market keep on every day Bantam one in the forenoon and two in the afternoon that especial which be keep in the forenoon do so abound with people that they throng together as in many fair in England yet I never see any kind of cattle to sell by reason that there be very few tame in the country their food be altogether Rice with some hen their food and some fish but not much or in no abundance the javan house be altogether build of great cane and some few small Timbers be slight building in many of the principal man house their house be good workmanship show as car^ings etc. and some of the chief have a square brick room be build in no better form than a brick-kiln which be only to put in all their household stuff when fire come but they seldom or never lodge nor eat in they there be many small river run through the town also there be a good road for ship whereby if they be people of any reasonable capacity it will be make a very goodly city also it be wall round with a brick wall be very warlike build with flanker and turret scour every way I have be tell by some that it be first build by the chiness in many place it be fall to decay for want of repair at the very end of this town be the China town a narrow river part they which run cross the end of the China town up to the king court and so through the middle of the great town and do ebb and flow so that at a high water both galley and junct of great burden may go up to the middle of the great town this China town be for the most part build of Brick every house square and flat overhead the China town some of they have board and small Timbers or s^lit cane over-crosse on which be lay brick and sand to defend they from fire over these brick warehouse be set a shed be build up with great cane and thatch and some be build up with small timber but the great number with cane only of late year since we come thither many man of wealth have build their house to the top all fire free of the which sort of house at our first come there be no more but the sabindar house and the rich china merchant house which nevertheless by mean of their window and shed ro^nd about they have be consume with fire in this town stand the english and dutch house which be build in the same manner the dutch and english house only they be very much big and high than ordinary house and the dutchman of late though with great cost and trouble have build one of their house up to the top all of brick fire free as they suppose the king of this place be absolute the king and his power punishment of adultery and since the depose and death of the late emperor of Damacke be hold the principal king of all that island he use always martial law upon any offender who he be dispose to punish if any private man wife or wi^es be take with dishonesty so that they have good proof of it they cause they present to be put to death both the woman and the man that be take in adultery with she and for their slave they may execute they for any small fault to every wife that a be a freeman marry costly wife he must keep ten women-slave which they as ordinary use as their wife and some of they keep for every wife forty slave for so they keep ten they may have as many more as they will but they may have but three wife only the javan be general exceed proud although extreme poor javans proud and poor by reason that not one among a hundred of they will work the gentleman of this land be bring to be poor by the number of slave that they keep which eat fast than their pepper or Rice grow the Chinois do both plant dr^sse and gather the pepper Chinois frugal and also sow their rice live as slave under they but they suck away all the wealth of the land by reason that the javan be so idle and a javan be so proud that he will not endure one to ^t a inch in height above he if he be but of the like call they be a people that do very much thirst after blood yet they will seldom fight face to face one with another or with any other nation but do altogether seek revenge of their enemy cowardly albeit they be for the most part man of a goodly stature their law for murder be to pay a fine to the king punishment of murder and that but a small sum but evermore the friend of the party murder will be revenge on the murderer or his kindred so that the more they kill one another the more fine have their King their ordinary weapon which they wear be call a ^rise it be about two foot in length their weapon and fight the bla^e be wave and crooked to and fro indenture like and withal exceed sharp most of they have the temper of their mettle poison so that not one among five hundred that be wound with they in the body escape with his life the handle of these weapon be either of horn or wood curious carve in the the likeness of a devil which many of they do worship in their war their fight be altogether with pike dart and target of late some few of they have learned to use their piece but very untoward the apparel of the be^ter sort be a tuck on their head and about their loin a fair pintadoe all the rest of their body naked sometime they will wear a close coat their apparel somewhat like a mandilion of velvet chamblet cloth or some other kind of silk but it be but seldom and upon some extraordinary occasion the common sort wear on their head a flat cap of velvet taffeta or c^llico-cloath the which be cut in many piece and seam with a fair stitch to make they sit flat and compass about their loin they wear a kind of callico-cloth which be make at Clyn in manner of a silk girdle but at the least one yard broad be of two colour also there come from thence many sort of white colour which they themselves do both die paint and gilled according to the fashion of that country likewise they can wear a kin^ of stripe stuff both of Cotten and rind of tree but by mean of their laziness there be very little of that wear their head and head-tire the man for the most part have very thick curl hair on their head in which they take great pride and often will go bareheaded to show their hair the woman go all bareheaded some of they have their hair tuck up like a carthorse tail but the better sort do tuck it up like our ride gelding tail about their loin they wear the same stuff which I have before mention always have a fair girdle or Pintado of their country fashion throw over on their shoulder which hang down loose behind they their religion the principal of they be most religious but they very seldom go to church they do acknowledge Christ to be a great prophet who they call Naby Isa and some of they do keep of Mahomet priest in their house but the common people have very little knowledge in any religion only they say there be a god which make heaven and earth and they also he be good they say and will not hurt they but the devil be naught and will do they hurt wherefore many of they for want of knowledge do pray to he the devil pray to only for fear lest he shall hurt they and sure if there be man of learning which be perfect in their language to instruct they a number of they will be draw to the true faith of Christ and also will be bring to civility for many which I have reason with concern the law of christian have like all well except only their plurality of woman for they be all very lascivious give bribe both man and woman the better sort which be in authority be great taker of bribe and all the javan in general be bad paymaster when they be trust notwithstanding their law for debt be so strict law for debt that the creditor may take his debtor his wife child slave and all that he have and sell they for his debt thievish people likewise they be all much give to steal from the high to the low and sure in time past they have be * * so l. Vertomannus idleness man-eater before that traffic be have with they by the Chynasses which as I have hear some of they say be not above one hundred year since they delight much in ease and music and for the most part they spend the day sit across legged like a tailor whitle of a stick whereby many of they become very good carver to carve their Crise handle and that be all the work that most of they endeavour to do they be very great eater but the gentleman allow their slave nothing but rice sod in water with some root and herb and they have a certain herb call bettaile which they usual have carry with they wheresoever they go in box or wrap up in a cloth like a sugarloaf and also a nut call pinange which be both in operation very hot and they eat they continual to warm they within and keep they from the flux they do likewise take much tobacco and also opium javans dull the javan themselves be very dull and blockish to manage any affair of a commonwealth whereby all stranger go beyond they that come into their land and many of the country of Clyn which come thither to dwell do grow very rich and rise to great office and dignity among they as their sabandar their laytamougon and other especial the chinese who like jew live crooch under they but rob they of their wealth and send it for China Chinois crafty the chinese be very crafty people in trade use all kind of cozen and deceit which may possible be devise they have no pride in they nor will refuse any labour except they turn javans as many of they do when they have do a murder or some other villainy than they be every whit as proud religion of the Chinois and as lazy as the javan for their religion they be of diverse sect but the most of they be atheist and many of they hold opinion that when they die if they be good man they shall be bear again to great riches and be make governor and if they be wicked man than they shall be turn into some ugly beast as a frog or a toad they burn sacrifice every new moon mumble prayer over they with a kind of sing voice and as they sing they thing a little bell which at the end of every prayer they ring out as fast as they can this ceremony they also use when any among they of account lie a die the manner of their sacrifice be this they furnish their altar with goat hen duck and diverse sort of fruit the which be sometime dress to eat and sometime raw and then be dress afterward and eat all that they burn be only paper paint and cut out in curious work and value by they at a certain price I have many time ask they to who they burn their sacrifice and they have answer i to God but the goserats and turk * * this seem to be the malice of one idolater to another which be there say they burn it to the devil if they do so they be ashamed to confess it they be many of they well see in astronomy and keep a good account of their month and year they observe no sabbath nor one day better than other except when they lie the foundation of a house or begin some other great work which day they ever after observe as a holy day when any of they that be wealthy die in Bantam their body be burn to ash funeral rite which ash they put close in jar and carry it to China to their friend I have see when some of they have lie a die they have set up seven odour burn four of they be great and burn light and they be set upon a cane which lie cross upon two crotche about six foot from the ground and three set on the ground right under they be very small and burn dim I have demand the meaning of it many time but I can never have other answer but that it be the fashion of China and sure many such like thing they do not know why or wherefore but only that it have be a fashion among they they delight very much in play and sing play but they have the worst voice that one shall hear any people have the which play or interlude they hold as service to their god in the begin of which they often use to burn a sacrifice the priest many time kneel down and kiss the ground three time one present after another these play be make common when they think their junck or ship be set forth from China likewise when they be arrive at Bantam and also when they set out from Bantam towards China these play sometime begin at noon and end not till the next day morning be most common in the open street have stage set up for the purpose moreover they have among they some soothsayer which sometime rage and run up and down the street like mad man soothsayer have sword draw in their hand tar their hair and throw themselves against the ground when they be in this frantic take they affirm and other chyneses do believe that they can tell what shall come to pass after whether they be possess with the devil or no who reveal something to they I know not but many chyneses use they when they send a juncke of any voyage to know whether they shall speed well or no and by their report it have fall out according as these soothsayer have tell they the chyneses be apparel in long gown wear kirtle under they hang something low than their gown they be sure the most effeminate and cowardly people that live effeminateness on their head they wear a cawl some of they be make of silk and some of hair the hair of their head be very long which they bind up on a knot right on the crown of their head their nobility and governor wear hood of sundry fashion some be one half like a hat and the other like a french-hood other be of network with a high crown and no brim feature of body these people be tall and strong of body have all very small black eye and very few of they have any hair on their face they will steal and do any kind of villainy to get wealth their manner at Bantam be to buy women-slave for they bring no woman out of China by who they have many child and when they return to their own country not mind to come to Bantam again they sell their woman but their child they carry with they as for their good they take a order to send some at every ship for if they die in Bantam all the good they have there be the king and if once they cut their hair hair cut they may never return to their country again but their child may always provide that they never cut their hair @. 2 a true and brief discourse of many danger by fire and other perfidious treachery of the javan after our ship be lade and all thing set in as good order as it can be upon the one and twentieth of February 1602. our general take his leave of the shore depart the english leave at Bantam mr. starkey leave behind he to be resident in Bantam nine person over who he appoint m. fifty six chest and fardel of good upon the six of march at night she set sail but by reason of contrary wind after she have spend near two month beat up and down in the sea she be force to return again to Bantam also at our general departure he leave we two house full of good and likewise some good lie in the Dutchman house but we be too few in number to keep one well have not God of his great mercy preserve we it be not unknown to all that be there the quarrel betwixt the javan and we before our ship depart who seek all the mean they can to be revenge insomuch javan go about to fire the english house that present after the departure of our pinnace they begin to practice the fire of our principal house with fiery dart and arrow in the night and not content with that but in the day time if we have bring out any quantity of good to air we shall be sure to have the town fire to windward not far from we and if these fire arrow have not by God providence be espy by some of our own house as they be it be think of we all that that house and good have be all consume as may plain appear at the top when we come to repair it but as the malice of the rascal sort of people begin now to there be a crew that mean to enter sudden upon we and to cut our throat in so much that we be but four at that house what with overwatching and what with the disease that reign much in that country which be looseness of the body we be grow to very great weakness and two of we never recover it the nineteen of April 1603. come into the road nine sail of hollander over who be general Wyborne Van the fleming about this time spread a rumour through their own fleet that the king will force we to lend he five thousand rial of eight otherwise he will cause our house to be pluck down again the wherefore a javan be slave to one of the principal of the country throw some firework upon a thatch house a little to windward of we javan treachery we espy it pursue he and take he and carry he to have die neither do we great seek it because his master be our very good friend also likewise if a javan do offend he must be punish with death for if they inflict any less punishment they be so wicked and bloody a people that they will be cowardly revenge not only of stranger but of their own master so that if any slave do offend his master he do quite forgive he or else he die for it but they be very obedient and will seldom offend their master because they be for the most part as wicked as themselves the two and twenty of August at night there be certain javan get into a great yard hard by our house who when we be sing of a psalm which we do use to do when we set our watch these rogue throw stone at our window as if they will have beat down our house and some of the stone come in at the window and miss we very narrow but we take some of they which yet upon submission we spare about this time there grow a quarrel between the fleming and the Chinois quarrel betwixt Chinois and hollander hollanders drunken disorder and some be slay and hurt on both side this grow by the misbehaviour of the fleming which in that place do carry themselves very rude and disorder in that abundant manner that they be a shame and infamy to Christendom and christian I do not condemn they all but the vulgar sort who when they be ashore and their drink in their commander can bear no rule over they they get the worst before this quarrel be end but not by the Chinois nor by manhood of the javan only some that be slave to some turncoat Chinois will steal behind the fleming in the evening and cowardly stab they one day they be very importunate for one of their man which be slay the protector demand of they when they come to any country to trade whether they bring law^s with they or
