hard by the town and be in all point like unto the javan will bold come into the town and not only in the evening and night come into house and cut off the people head but at noon day in so much that for the space of a month we can take little rest forth grievous cry of the people one day while we be sit at dinner they come and take a woman be our next neighbour and muffle she so with a sack that she can not cry and so carry she into a tuft of bush in our backside and there cut her throat and mean to have cut off her head if they have have time her husband miss she and look out may see they carry she who cry out and we rise from dinner and pursue they but it be too late to save her life also they be very swift of foot so that we can come near none of they and for any thing that we know they may be among we for after the javan be come we can not know they it be think of some that they lay hide in the bush till the come of the javan and then steal out and put themselves among they there be some java woman that will cut off their husband head in the night perfidious javan and sell they to these people they do linger much about our house and sure if we have not keep good watch they will have attempt the cut of our throat if not for our head for our good but after awhile many of they be know and be take be execute which be man of very goodly stature the reason they do make these hard adventure cruelty reward be their king give they a woman for every stranger head they bring he wherefore many time they will dig up such as be new bury at Bantam and cut off their head and so cozen their King also at this time some credible man that wish we well of who the admiral be one bid we have a special care of our good watch because some of the principal of the land in birth though not in wealth nor office treachery intend and prevent which have many slave but little to maintain they have lay a plot to have slay we in the night and to have make spoil of our good which they take to be ten time more than be and after to have give it out the lampoon have do it whereupon we be force to have light burn all night round about our house otherwise in the dark night they be so black as they be may have enter sudden upon we before we shall descry they for all the upper work of our house by reason of the heat be open and they be build with cane and likewise the fence round about the house which be but a weak building and may quick be bear down these heathen devil come forth two or three time think to have execute their bloody pretence but God will not suffer they for so soon as they come within sight of our light and may hear our drum sound at the end of every watch their hear^s fail they so that they dare not give the attempt for they suppose we be ready not only themselves and so be disperse diverse other make bold but vain attempt and therefore now fall to work with the Chinois who house at this time be full of our good which they have buy in so much that everynight for a long time we have such grievous cry out and we look every hour when we shall be assault dare take no rest in the night many Chinois about we be slay and sure if we have not defend they with our shot many more will have be slay for the sing of a bullet be as terrible to a javan as the cry of the hound be in the ear of the hare for they will not abide if once they hear it but these continual alarm and grievous outcry of man woman and child grow so rife in our ear the misery of the English that our man in their sleep will dream they be pursue the javan and sudden will leap and if they shall have set their weapon further from they they will not have be ready if we shall have have occasion the which we look for every minute and be but few of we I take my turn to watch as they will urge the rest of the Chinois to help we pluck out pack promise they shall be well pay for their pain it please God to put so much good in their mind which I think never have any before nor and therefore will not work any more and the next day be pay for their work beside what they steal discovery of knavery we wonder much how this fire shall come suspect the portugal have hire malaye to hide in a privy and this be he that put the fire to our house he be a goldsmith and confess to the admiral he have clip many ryalls and also coin some counterfeit some thing he confess to he concern our matter but not much but he will tell we nothing wherefore because of his sullenness and that it be he that f^red we I cause he to be burn under the nail of his thumb finger and toe with sharp hot iron and the nail to be tear off and because he never blinsh at that cruel torture we think that his hand and leg have be numb with tie wherefore we burn he in the hand arm shoulder and neck but all be one with he then we burn he quite through the hand and with rasphe of iron tear out the flesh and sinew after that I cause they to knock the edge of his shinbone with hot fear iron a dissolute resolution then I cause cold screw of iron to be screw into the bone of his arm and sudden to be snatch out after that all the bone of his finger and toe to be break with pincer yet for all this he never shed tear no nor once turn his head aside nor stir hand nor foot but when we demand any question he will put his tongue between his tooth and strike his chin upon his knee to bite it off when all the extremity we can use be but in vain I cause he to be put fast in iron again where the amit or aunt which do great abound there get into his wound and torment he worse than we have do as we may well see by his gesture the king officer desire i he may be shoot to death I tell they that be too good a death for such a villain and say more that in our country if a gentleman or a soldier have commit a iact worthy of death than he be shoot to death and yet he be befriend too but they do hold it to be the cruel and base death that be wherefore they be very importunate in the evening we lead he into the field and make he fast to a stake the first shoot carry away a piece of his arm bone and all execution the next shot strike he through the breast up near to the shoulder than he hold down his head look upon the wound the three shot that be make one of our man have cut a b^llet in three part which stroke upon his breast in a triangle whereat he fall down as low as the stake will give he leave but between our man and the fleming they shoot he almost all to piece before they leave he now in this time the admiral and the Sabyndar send we a guard of man every night for fear the Chynois a mischief whatsoever come of it and I see it for the king and the governor have send to he often time to deliver we that fellow he have but he care not for they short after we have many shrewd attempt to have fire our house for the town be fire in three place at one instant in the night a little to windward of our house often treachery a woman steal and twice another night but God bless our industry and preserve we among all these sorrowful and troublesome discourse it happen that a certain Chynois which dwell hard under our pale do steal away another chyny wife and be hardly pursue by her husband they have no mean to shift she away but to put she over the pale into our ground and at that time we have new shoot much pepper into our warehouse which be so extreme hot the heat of pepper in those part that we be force to keep the door open night and day have always a regard to it in the night this be a fit place for she to hide she in get behind the door so far as she can stand for heat and her husband will have seek all java and china before he will or dare come thither to seek in the night after our watch be set one of our company go into our backside the which place we do very much frequent night and day but as he be come back and be a little star light he see the woman stand in the pepper house door who come forth to take breath for she have be better to have be in the stove so long he present swear a woman I run down and cause she to be search and examine present a merry jest she tell we that her husband will have beat she wherefore she be force to climb over our pale and to hide herself it be a ordinary thing for the chine to beat their wife especial she be a cuchinchyne woman which have no friend in town for the javan will hardly suffer they to beat their woman wherefore now have search and secure every place I think it will prove but some such jest. the next morning her husband come who fall down on his marie-bone desire i to be good unto he for I have so late torture some chine he think I will torture he but in my conscience he need no more plague or punishment then such a wife wherefore I present dismiss they both the protector a little before have give we all the house and ground which join to our pale and belong to those chynois which undermine our house but although it be give yet I think there be never Englishman pay so dear for so little ground in any country in the world the house be rot but the ground do we great pleasure we buy also a house of a pangran or gentleman which come so near our pepper-house door that it be very troublesome to we when we shall carry in or out our pepper wherefore I buy that house with the ground so that now we have a very spacious yard the nine of September the protector send a proclamation that no chine shall weigh any pepper to the stranger mean the english and the hollander the which proclamation be procure by the hollander and we know it very well for the same day they dine with we and at dinner they tell we the protector owe they ten thousand sack of pepper but I tell they that be not so the old queen for they will never be such fool to trust he so much the next morning I go to the old woman who command the protector and all the rest and indeed be call queen of the land by the sabindar and diverse other although she be not of the king blood but only for her wisdom be hold in such estimation among they of all sort that she rule as if she be sole queen of that country after we have make our grief know to she she present send for the protector will we to talk with he before she when he come I demand of he for what cause he have forbid we to trade he answer he must buy ten thousand sack of pepper for the king I tell he again that the fleming themselves tell i that the our yard which be our court of guard that escape where we encamp by night the dutch house escape dutch enemy in trade otherwise friend though but narrow wherefore we borrow some of their man for it be we with our drum shot and pike live a soldier life until our fence be make up and afterward too for this be but to show we the way and our fence be no soon up but we look every hour when it shall be burn down or bear down by those that will have have the cut of our throat the pangran mandelicko in the end of September fall to rob of junck one of which be of lade with rice man and woman with a but be all traitor to the king maintain he so that the king officer dare not meddle with he the protector Sabindar and admiral send to we to take heed to ourselves the rebel grow every day strong and colour and also their music which be ten or twelve pan of Tombaga carry upon a coulstaffe between two these be tuneable and every one a note above another and always two go by they which be skilful in their country music and play on they have thing in their hand of purpose to strike they also they have another kind of music which go both afore and after but these pan be the principal after the pike follow a crew of targeteer with dart than be bring in many sort of tree with their fruit grow upon they than follow many sort of beast and fowl both alive and also artificial make that except one have be near they be not to be discern from those that be alive after these follow a crew attire like masker which before the king do dance vault dancer and tumbler and show many strange kind of tumble trick of these there be both man and woman after all these follow sometime two hundred sometime three hundred woman all carry present only at every ten woman there go a old motherly woman soldier to keep they in order which carry nothing these present be of Rice and cash present the which be lay in frame make of split cane curious set out for show with paint and gild paper but the present itself be not common worth above twelve penny or thereabouts after they follow the rich present which be common a fair Tuck and some fair cloth of their country fashion be curious wrought and guild or embroider with gold for the king own wear the which be carry also by woman have two pike bear upright before they also every present which be for the king wear have a rich Tierasoll bear over it last javan who can endure to have any stand over they will remove a good distance from we and many of the king guard forsake their weapon and will go sit afar off neither can they endure that one shall lay his hand on their head the which be not for any point of religion as some will affirm but only of mere pride many time when I have come into a chinees house where javan have set in the floor I sit down on a chest as our order be they have all start up and run out at door the chinees will tell we if any other nation shall do so but we or the hollander they will stab they but they dare not meddle person about he so soon as ever he come in sight the king guard all rise up and every man prove his weapon the which we have never see before when any show come in so that it shall seem that there be great fear not that the king of jacatra will offer any violence but there be a number of other petty king who have great troop of man many petty king the which king be his mortal enemy wherefore fear I go accompany with my merchant and other in the best manner I can befit for the honour of my king and country at my come on shore after their barbarous manner I be kind receive and multitude of people follow i all desirous to see a new come people much nominate but never come in their part as I be near the governor house word be bring i that he be not well but I think rather drink with he have writer who by turn set down every thing in write which he do so that there be nothing pass in his life time which be not note no not so much as his go to the necessary and how often he lie with his woman and with who and all this be do unto this end that when he die these writing of all his action and speech the mogul make his brother child christian this christianity be since disclaim and be then but a trick rather of sensuality than of devotion or state which be worthy to be set down may be record in the chronicle at my be with he he make his brother child christian the do whereof be not for any zeal he have to christianity as the father and all christian think but upon the prophecy of certain learned gentile who tell he that the son of his body shall be disinherit and the child of his brother shall reign and therefore he do it to make these child hateful to all moor as christian be odious in their sight and that they be once christian when any such matter shall happen they shall find no subject but God be omnipotent and can turn the make of these christian unto a good end if it be his pleasure this king among his child have one call sultan shariar of seven year of age and his father on a day be to go some whether to solace himself demand of he whether he will go with he the child answer that if it please his highness he will either go or stay as the pleasure of his father be but because his answer be not that withal his heart he will wait upon his majesty he be very well buffet by the king and that in such sort that no child in the world but will have cry which this child do not wherefore his father demand why he cry not he answer that his nurse tell he that it be the great shame in the world for prince to cry when they be beat and ever since they nurture i in this kind say he I never cry and nothing shall make i cry to the death upon which speech his father be more vex strike he again and cause a bodkin to be bring he which he thrust through his cheek but all this will not make he cry although he bleed very much which be admire of all that the father shall do this unto his child and that he be so stou^ that he will not cry there be great hope of this child to exceed all the rest this emperor keep many feast in the year^ but two feast especial may be nominate two feast the one call the no^^ous which be in honour of the new-year day this feast continue eighteen day and the wealth and riches be wonderful that be to be see in the deck and set forth of every man room or place where he lodge when it be his turn to watch for every nobleman have his place appoint he in the palace in the midst of that spacious place I speak of there be a rich yent pitch but so rich a exceed rich tent. that I think the like can be find in the world this tent be curious wrought and have many Seminans join round about it of most curious wrought velvet embroider with gold and many of they be of cloth of gold and silver these Seminans be shadow to keep the sun from the compass of this tent. I may say it be at the least two acre of ground but so rich spread with silk and gold carpet and hang in the principal place rich as rich velvet embroider with gold pearl and precious stone can make it within it five chair of estate be place most rich to behold where at his pleasure the king sit there be likewise private room make for his queen most rich where they sit and see all but be not see so round about this tent the compass of all may be some five acre of ground every principal nobleman make his room and deck it likewise every man according to his ability strive who may adorn his room rich the king where he do affect come to his nobleman room and be most sumptuous feast there and at his departure be present with the rare jewel and toy that they can find but because he will not receive any thing at that time as a present he command his treasurer to pay what his praiser value they to be worth which be value at half the price every one and all of his noble provide toy and rare thing to give he at this feast so common at this feast every man his estate be augment two day of this feast the better sort of the woman come to take the pleasure thereof and this feast begin at the begin of the moon of March the other feast be some four month after which be call the feast of his birthday the feast of his birthday this day every man strive who may be the rich in apparel and jewel after many sport and pastime perform in his palace he go to his mother house with all the better sort of his noble where every man present a jewel unto his mother according to his estate after the banquet be end the king go into a very fair room where a balance of beat gold be hang with one scale empty for he to sit in the other scale be fill with diverse thing that be to say silver gold diverse sort of grain a little and so of every kind of mettle a little and with all sort of precious stone some in fine he weigh himself with these thing which the next day be give to the poor and all may be value to be worth * * see hereof sir thom. roe ten thousand pound this day before he go unto his mother house every man bring he his present which be think to be ten time more worth then that which he give to the poor this do every man depart unto his home his custom be that when you petition he for any thing you must not come empty hand but give he some toy or other whether you write or no by the gift you give he he know that you will demand some thing of he so after enquiry be make if he see it convenient he grant it the custom of the indian be to burn their dead as you have read in other author and at their burn many of their wife will burn with they voluntary burn of woman with their dead husband because they will be register in their book for famous and most modest and love wife who leave all worldly affair content themselves to live no long than their husband I have see many proper woman bring before the king who by his commandment none may burn without his leave and sight of they I mean those of agra when any of these come he do persuade they with many promise of gift and live if they will live but in my time no persuasion can prevail but burn they will the king see that all will not serve give his leave for she to be carry to the fire where she burn herself alive with her dead husband likewise his custom be when any great nobleman have be absent from he two or three year if they come in favour and have perform well he receive they in manner and form follow first the nobleman stay at the gate of the palace till the and lieutenant general and knight Martial come to accompany he unto the king favourable entertainment of the then he be bring to the gate of the outermost rail whereof I have speak before where he stand in the view of the king in the midst between these two noble then he touch the ground with his hand and also with his head very grave and do thus three time this do he kneel down touch the ground with his forehead which be once do he be carry forward towards the king and in the midway he be make to do this reverence again then he come to the door of the red rail do the like reverence the three time and have thus do he come within the red rail and do it once more upon the carpet then the king command he to come up the stair or ladder of seven step that he may embrace he where the king most love embrace he before all the people whereby they shall take notice that he be in the king favour the king have do this he than come down and be place by the lieutenant general according to his degree now if he come in disgrace through exclamation make against he he have none of these honour from the king but be place in his place till he come to his trial this king be very much adore of the heathen commonalty insomuch that they will spread their body all upon the ground rub the earth with their face on both side they use many other foppery and superstition which I omit leave they for other traveller which shall come from thence hereafter after I have write this there come into my memory another feast solemnize at his father funeral funeral feast or obit for his father which be keep at his sepulchre where likewise himself with all his posterity mean to be bury upon this day there be great store of victual dress and much money give to the poor this sepulchre may be count one of the rare monument of the world it have be this fourteen year a building and it be think it will not be finish these seven year more in end gate and wall and other needful thing for the beautify and set of it forth the least that work there daily be three thousand people but thus much I will say sumptuous sepulchre that one of our workman will dispatch more than three of they the sepulchre be some @ of a mile about make square it have seven height build every height narrow than the other till you come to the top where his hearse be at the outermost gate before you come to the sepulchre there be a most stately palace building the compass of the wall join to this gate of the sepulchre and guard be within may be at the least three mile this sepulchre be some four mile distant from the city of agra chap. 8 the voyage of Mr DAVID MIDDLETON in the consent a ship of one hundred and fifteen tun which fall forth from Tilburie hope on the twelve of march 1606. the 16. of july 1607. we anchor in the road of Saldania all our man in good health only Peter Lambert the day before fall off the top-most head whereof he die the one and twenty the captain and master go to Pengwin island three league distant from the road where we see such abundance of seal and pengwin that it be admirable for you may drive five hundred pengwin together in a flock and thousand of seal together upon the shore the island be not above some three mile long and some two mile broad but in my opinion there be not a island in the world more frequent with fowl and seales then this island it have pengwin wild-goose duck drake and pelican and diverse other fowl and after some pleasure take there we return again unto our ship have buy some cattle and end all our business and our man well refresh we weigh anchor the nine and twenty day about four of the clock in the morning with very little wind and come out of the road of Saldania our man in very good health and loath to depart without the company of our admiral and vice-admiral but we be not certain of their arrival there which make we make so little stay so direct our course for s. Laurence we leave Saldania the thirty day calm all day till three of the clock in the afternoon and then we have a fresh gale at south-west and we steer away half a watch south and by west and two watch and a half southeast and at ten of the clock at night the cape Bona Esperansa bare north of we and all that night blow very much wind and the sea much grow and the ship come betwixt twelve of the clock at night and twelve of the clock next day be the one and thirty of july nine and twenty league all this day a very pleasant gale sometime rain we come four league from the cape August 1. 1607 cape agullis north fifty five fathom the first of August we have very fair weather sometime a gale and sometime calm continue so all day and we steer away two watch southeast and by east and three watch at east and by south the wind variable sometime at south and sometime at south by east dark weather and she run some one and twenty league than we be in five and thirty degree and twenty two minute of height the seven and twenty of August the wind at northwest and we steer away east and by south and at two of the clock we see the land of s. Laurence or Madagascar by estimation some six league off and then we steer away north and by west and at noon we observe and make the ship to be in twenty four degree and forty minute the variation at night sixteen degree and twenty three minute the thirty at five of the clock in the afternoon we anchor in the bay of s. Augustine in six fathom and a half great gravel and we be enforce to go to lee-ward bay of s. Augustine be to the roome-ward of the road before we can get in by reason of a great breach that lie off the bay and then come in close upon a tack and have in come in seven six and a half and five fathom all the way and come very fair by the breach and rid in the road with two land in the wind of we and the breach both the one and thirty day our captain with m. davis go in our long boat to view the land and I myself as we go sound close aboard the breach and have six fathom one of the land be very small as it be a bank of sand and nothing on it the other be about a mile in length and half a mile in breadth and nothing upon it but some small store of wood. the first of September 1607. we weigh anchor from our first place and come within two mile of the mouth of the river and rid in five fathom and a half very fast ground for where we ride before it be very foul ground so that we break one of our cable in the weigh I judge it to be some three league from our first place where we have urey foul ground the seven day have end all our business be provide of wood and water and all thing else we weigh anchor in the morning about five of the clock a mark on shore most like a barn or a long house with the wind at east and by north a pleasant gale and we steer away come out west and west and by north till we be clear of the breach and we bring to sea with we four goat three sheep and a young heifer here we find great plenty of victual both sheep and beef for little value this day we observe some three mile from the island before the bay of s. Augustine and we make it to be in twenty three degree and forty eight minute of latitude and after we be clear of the breach which lie to the northward of the island we steer away south Southwest and south and by west sometime with very fair weather the wind at southeast and by east a pleasant gale the eleven a fresh gale at southeast and southeast and by east and we stand into the shore till midnight and then we see a great breach right a head hard by we but we hear the rut before we see it God be praise and so we tackd and stand off again present and at noon observe and make the ship to be in twenty five degree and twenty two minute of latitude the twelve of November in the morning we see a island and stand to make it and find it to be Ingana and come to the north-side of it the island be in length five league or thereabot it lie east and by south and west and by north the easter end be the high land and the wester end be full of tree it lie in latitude in five degree and a half and the variation be four degree and thirteen minute so after we have make it have the wind at west northwest we steer away for the main of sumatra east and by south and east southeast a pleasant gale but very much rain so the thirteen day in the morning Novemb. 13. 1607. we see the main land of sumatra some four league from we the fourteen we anchor in Bantam roade about four of the clock in the afternoon be Saturday where we find the merchant in very good health and all thing in good order the next day our captain go on shore and speak with m. Towerson concern the ship business and agree to have our iron and lead a shore which we bring with we which be effect with some roomage and have fit our ship in good order and take in merchandise and our merchant for the with leave take of the merchant we set sail from Bantam ride the six of December 1607. with little wind and come out of the road decemb. 6. 1607. and anchor that night in sight of the high land of Bantam the next day weigh in the morning and sail with a prosperous wind still continue fair pass many land and sink ground some night we sail and othersome lay a hull rain thunder and lightning be no strange thing to we in those part but one comfort we have that God give we a fair wind wherewith we sail merry on our intend voyage in the begin of januarie they arrive at the the rest of this month be spend in entertainment and compliment betwixt we and the spaniard as likewise with the moluccan prince so be the whole month of February also the reason be the spaniard dare not admit we trade till the camp master have give leave and he in those broil betwixt he and the hollander except we will do or seem to do some piece of service at least accompany their ship for great show which our captain absolute refuse be against his commission excuse himself mean while they have privy trade with the people by night and be jovial and frolic by day with the spaniard which both give and receive kind welcome in the begin of march they be permit open trade but this within few day be countermand and we command to be go and thus they spend the time till march the fourteen when they weigh anchor and set sail some trade they have also in the way this part of the journal be long and I have omit it as elsewhere in those thing which I think may be tedious the three and twenty 1608. we enter the straits of Bangaya whereunto have enter march 23. 1608. straits of Bangaya our captain determine to send off his long boat to seek for water for here he purpose to store himself therewith while he be thus determine there come a praw off from the island with all the speed he can make who come unto we and speak with we of who we demand whether there be any fresh water in that island who make answer that if our captain please he will bring we to very good water whereupon we stand over for the east shore and anchor about one of the clock in the afternoon in sixty fathom of water where there run a most cruel current then after we come to anchor fit our long boat with cask we go with the indian to fetch water where while they be fit the boat he sell some fresh fish for China dish very cheap so at night our man come aboard and bring very good water but have a wearisome rowth of it be five mile distant from the place where we anchor the four and twenty in the morning we go again for a other boat lade of water and this morning by day break there come of the country people above one hundred prawe man and woman and bring we fish both dry fish and fresh fish very good of both kind great plenty and very cheap they bring we also hog great and small which they sell we for course white cloth and hen and cock in abundance at the like price some for China dish and some for cloth they bring we also fruit as Cassathoe root and diverse other fruit and stay aboard we all day that sometime we be not able to stir up and down the ship for they in the afternoon the king send our captain some and Irea to drink which be a kind of water call by that name our captain give the messenger great thanks in his king behalf and to requite his kindness send he a rich Pintado then he depart and all the rest and about ten of the clock at night we weigh anchor and in the weigh we break both our starboard anchor flook then sail away with very little wind at length man our long boat and tow our ship all night for if we have not tow she in this calm we have be drive to lee-ward more than we shall have get again in three day without a fresh gale of wind the current run so strong there the nineteen of April the king of Buttone send one of his brother again to know whether our captain be willing he shall come aboard king of Buttone for he be very desirous to see both he and our ship because he have hear much of englishman but never see any our captain send he word that he shall think himself much grace if he come present the king come off in his Caricoll row at least with a hundred oar have in she beside about four hundred man with arm^s well appoint to fight and six brass piece and in her company five caricol more which have at the least a thousand man in they so richard rowles lieutenant general with the discovery of the redde-sea in the ascension @. i. relation of the say voyage write by THOMAS JONES in a unfortunate hour the fourteen day of march in the year of our lord 1607. with the two tall ship the ascension and the union we weigh anchor at Woolwich the six of may 1608. have spend some day in refresh our man at maio we direct our course for the pass of the equinoctial and so for the cape of Bona Speranza southeast and by south and south southeast the equinoctial we pass very speedy and then you have the general wind that blow continual between the southeast and southeast and by east so that the further you sail to the southward you shall find the wind to easter the more as between the equinoctial and the tropic of Capricorn Palma a carack the eleven day of june in the latitude of six and twenty degree be under the tropic we meet with a carrack that be find for India her name be the nave Palma this carrack be cast away afterward upon the coast of Soffala within twelve league of mosambike the capt. hereof come home in a carack the captain of which say ship come passenger home in the same carrack that I come out of India in be admiral of the fleet of four sail so according to the custom of the sea have spend some compliment in friendly manner we depart from he to follow our voyage the thirteen of july we come to a anchor in the bay of Saldania and stay there unto the five and twenty of September the bay of Saldania in build of a pinnace at which time the westerly monsons have do blow and then the wind blow more between the south and the southeast the five and twenty of September we come out of the bay and the six and twenty of the same month we be encounter with a mighty storm at the south southeast which blow so vehement that we split our fore-corse that night and lose the company of our consort the union and our pinnace call the good hope which we have build at the foresay cape and never hear of they afterward only the pinnace except which come to we to aden in the red-sea thus with contrary wind have before neglect our season of time we beat up and down the sea in follow our voyage unto the eighteen day of November before we can get the great island of s. Laurence but there we beat two day to get about cape s. Roman but can no^ this alter their mind that they bear up for the island of Comora Comora which stand betwixt the island of s. Laurence and the main in the southerly latitude of eleven degree the six and twenty day of October we come to a anchor on the westerside of the island in six and thirty fathom water here we be use of the king and people with all the kindness that may be but can get no fresh water yet have marvelous good refresh of limb and some hen and Coco nut which be a great comfort unto we the last day of the say month we weigh anchor and depart from the island of Comora and direct our course for the island of zanzibar mind there to relieve our want of water but through the default of our master we over-shot the island of zanzibar and fall with the island of Pemba have almost run ashore in the night before we do see it the wind be by the east north-east we cast about and stand off till day think it to be the island zanzibar when it be day we find a place on the southside of the island have a ledge of rock to the eastward of we here we ride in seven or eight fathom water be the seven day of December the latitude of the place be six degree to the southward be the south-west end of the island the eight of the say month I go ashore to seek for water of which we can not fill above six tun a day we ply our business with great recourse of the people and familiarity with we but all be in treachery have almost do our business and only lack some four or five ton of water to fill be the eighteen day I go ashore to fill those empty cask with water where against my come they have lay a ambush of some two hundred man which break out upon we yet praise be God treacherous people we do escape their hand only my servant John Harington except who they take and murder most cruel I not be able to rescue he also they wound a servant of John Elmors be one of our master mate but the youth recover of his wound be eleven in number also a little before they do put their treachery in practice one of the chief of they come unto i desire i to send one of our man with he to fetch a present for our general which I grant but the fellow never come again the youngman that go be bear in Greenwich his name be Edward churchman who afterward die in Mombasa of a bloudy-fluxe as I be credible inform of the portugal also while we make our abode at Pemba the portugal be about to man a flemish hulk which have winter in Mombasa to come to take our ship but hear of the force of our ship they alter their mind the people of this island o^ Pemba be very cowardly people and dare do nothing of themselves without the incite of the portugal we depart from thence the nineteen day of the say month determine to beat up between Pemba and the main of Melinda Melinda in hope to find the current the strong but that night to our great dismay we come aground upon the coast of Melinda but at that very instant the wind do lander so that with the back of our sail a stern our ship go off to our no little comfort so that night we stand to the eastward till day our ship praise be God have receive no harm at all when it be day we see certain showld that lie off the easter end of Pemba that we can not weather then we cast about and stand to the northward but in the end we have sight of three bark of moor which in their language they call pangay which we give chase unto with our ship and boats three pangay take and in the end fetch they up they strike sail without any resistance and with our boat we fetch they all aboard our ship who be in number fifty man or thereabouts these moor have think to have betray our ship as afterward do appear for the chief of they be in the cabin with our master and our chief merchant william revet and myself w revet stab he with his long knife which he have hide privy about he do stab our master Philip grove so sore that we have think he will not have live but contrary to the moor expectation I end his day in the place the rest of the moor likewise that be within the ship do at that very instant put their tragedy in practice in stab of our preacher and one of our merchant but praise be God in a small time we vanquish they all revenge so that there do not escape above five or six at the most to carry news of their fellow be a just revenge for our former wrong for when they do put this wickedness in practice we have not aboard our ship above fifteen or sixteen man at the most all the rest be employ in our boates. afterward I be credible inform by the portugal of the great lamentation which be make for these moor because they be of the chief gentleman of all the coast of Melinda and of the blood royal now after the spoil of these bark we determine to stay no long on the north side of Pemba so we put out of the west-end of the island again determine to beat up for the island of Socotora but the wind hang between the east and east southeast and find small help of the current do altogether frustrate our determination then we determine to stand off to the southward some two hundred or three hundred league think to find the wind at east southeast but here likewise we be frustrate of our hope for in the off we find the wind to hang at the east north-east and at the north-east and by east that we lie beat in the sea from the twenty day of December unto the six and twenty day of january and then it be our good hap to meet with certain land which we name the desolate land the desolate land not desolate of Coco nut and other provision because there be not any inhabitant upon they these land be at the least some twelve or thirteen in number and aught very diligent to be seek of they that shall travail hereafter because of the good refresh that be upon they water be there in great abundance also great store of Coco nut great store of fresh fish and likewise store of turtle-dove which be so tame that one man may take with his hand twenty dozen in a day also great store of palmeto-tree so that these land seem to we a earthly paradise have refresh ourselves at the aforesaid land we determine to follow our voyage but still be cross with contrary wind until the thirty day of march and then begin the westerly monsons than we get the island of Socotora but have espy a sail which be find for the red sea we give chase and in the end fetch they up be find for aden be glad of his company we consort with he and determine to go both in company together this ship do belong to Diu but he tell we that he do belong to surat tell we certain news of captain Hawkins and of his be at surat whereof we be very glad thus we hold on our determine course until the eight of April at which time we come to a anchor in the road of aden against the city aden this city of aden be under the dominion of the great Turk and be the key of all Arabia the same day we come thither the captain of the castle come aboard of we with twelve soldier to guard our general ashore where when he come he be receive with all the honour that may be not suffer he once scant to tread on the ground but mount he upon a fair arabian horse and so in triumph he be carry to the governor of the town where after kind entertainment the governor understanding that he have letter from the king majesty of England to the bashaw of Zenan our king letter to the basna of Zenan or Sinan their pinnace come also to aden John luffken murder who abode be fifteen day journey up into the country from aden whither they be send we remain in the road of aden until the ten day of May and then our pinnace the good hope which we have lose before at the cape of Bona esperanza come to we have endure great misery and they have murder most shameful their master John luffken because they say he will not put in with the shore to relieve they be then at the eastern end of saint Laurence but the chief cause be for his provision and the next day they put in with the shore and come to a anchor where they get both water and other provision but here they leave my servant Edward hill behind they Edward hill leave on land in s. Laurence who as they say go to cut wood can not be hear off the party that do the murder so soon as they come to we have their reward according to their desert be both execute aboard the pinnace where they do the murder who name be Thomas clerk who be his mate and Francis Driver gunner of the say pinnace thus we remain at aden until the fifteen of the say month and then our general and master determine to go for the city of Moka which stand up high in the red sea some forty league or thereabouts but at our departure from aden the governor do detain two of our merchant who name be John jordan and Philip glassecocke and certain cloth and so send they up altogether to the bassa John jordan and Philip glascocke go up to Zenan where when they come they be use most kind the bassa demand of they whether they have bring the great Turk his letter with they they answer he no whereupon he tell they he can not give they any leave to settle a factory but for the cloth which you have here I will take this for a present because your ship be the first of the english nation that ever come into these part and see you be come I give you leave to sell your good and buy what you will and so to depart at your pleasure custom free because of the cloth which I detain in my hand thus with much trouble because the westerly monson begin to come in they pass the straits of the red Sea and then the current run out of the red sea in the end we pass the straits be not above one mile and a half broad at the most the eleven of june we come to anchor in the road of Moka where we be most kind entertain and the same day our general go ashore where he be most love receive this city of Moka be the chief staple for all indian trade they arrive at Moka or Moha for all the good that be bring to cairo and to Alexandria come from thence we stay in this road of Moka in trim of our pinnace until the six and twenty day of july and then our general and master determine to follow their voyage for Cambaya sore against the mind of the company be the chief officer of the ship that night through the head-strongnesse of our master we lose two anchor the seven day of August we come to the island of Socotora where we have so much wind at south and south southeast that we be hardly able with our ship to keep the shore which our pinnace not be able to do be blow off have not above two or three day victual in she at the most while we lie at this island of Sacotora to get in a boat lade of water and two or three boat of stone for ballast we have such forcible gale of wind that we break two more of our best anchor have lose as be aforesaid two before in the red sea so vehement do those south-west wind blow at that island in that time of the year we now have but two left to supply our use withal we stay at the island of Socotora until the twenty day of August and then we weigh and direct our course for Cambaya septemb 1609 diu. the second day of September we fall with the coast of Diu some eight league to the eastward of Diu we steer alongst the shore some seven league more to the eastward and then come to a anchor a head-land the three day we send our Skiffe ashore where the people resort unto we have certain conference with they as also buy of they sheep and other thing they understanding that we be find for surat one of they come aboard desire of our general passage to surat as also certify our general that the way be very dangerous offer he for seven piece of eight to fetch a pilot which shall conduct the ship safe to the port. but be rule in most thing by our master he not regard the word of the aforesaid Moor or bannian the four day we weigh anchor about three of the clock in the afternoon at the last quarter ebb if we have take the first quarter flood we shall sure have have water over all those shall so that night we run on the shall and stroke our rudder off they run upon the shall of Cambaya and the next day be the five day of September we lose our ship also that night we forsake our ship and betake we to our two boat be a thing most miraculous that so many man shall be save in two such small boat we be at the least eighteen league from the shore thus be this tall ship lose to the great hindrance of the worshipful company and to the utter undo of all we the poor mariner be altogether overthrow with all the treasure and good both of the merchant and the poor company be so far from our native country Ascention lose we remain upon the sea in our boat until the six day about four of the clock in the afternoon and then we discover land which we make unto with all the mean we can possible endeavour the best we can to fall with the river of surat but note how the lord do preserve we have as I say before deliver we from the danger of the sea he will not now suffer we to fall into the hand of our enemy I mean the portugal who lie at that time at the bar of surat God merciful deliverance with five sail of frigate to take our boat at our come ashore for they have intelligence of our ship come before for contrary to our mind we fall with the river of Gandevee some five league to the southward of the bar of surat Gandeuce where we be kind entertain of the governor of the town here we hear likewise of the come of our pinnace into the same river and of she fetch away by the portugal but all the man have forsake she and be go to surat by land the governor of this town of Gandeuce be a Bannyan and one of those kind of people the town of Gandeuce that observe the law of Pythagoras they hold it a great sin to eat of any thing that have life or breath but live of that which the earth natural afford of itself they likewise honour the cow and have she in great estimation among they and also observe the ancient custom of burn of their dead it have likewise in old time be a great custom among they for the woman so soon as their husband be dead to burn themselves alive with he but now of late year they have learn more wit and do not use it so common yet those woman that do it not have their hair cut and ever after be hold for no honest woman for that they will not accompany their husband into the other world as they say the seven day we depart out of this town to travel for surat which may be some forty mile or thereabouts and the nine day come thither where William Finch keep the factory meet we but captain Hawkins be go up to the king to agra agra this city of agra be from surat some thirty day journey there the king be resident and keep his court. here at surat our general with our company stay till the latter end of September and then himself with the rest of our company go from surat and take their journey up for the city of agra so to travel by the way of Persia for England but I hold no fit course for i determine with myself to take some other course for the get into my country while I be in many determination it please God of his goodness to send a father of the order of saint Paul be a Portugal who be come from Cambaya to surat by land with who I come acquaint he promise i that if I will commit myself into his hand he will send i home into my country or at the leastwise into Portugal which promise he do accomplish most faithful in company of this father myself and three more of our company Richard mellis who die in the carrack in the way homeward find John Elmor and one Robert fox depart from surat the seven day of October and come into the strong town and fortress of daman daman Cha where once again I see our pinnace the good hope that we have build at the cape of Bona esperanza from daman we come to Chau from thence to Goa the eighteen day of November Goa our lady of pity the nine day of january we be embark in a carrack call our lady of pity be the admiral of the fleet of four sail and so depart the coast of India the eight and twenty day of january we pass the equinoctial upon the coast of India and the one and twenty of march we fall with the land in thirty three degree and a half some five league eastward of cape Agulas cape Agulas where we lie with contrary wind until the second of April and then we be encounter with a mighty storm at the west south-west which blow so vehement that we be force to bear up six hour before the sea and then it please God to send we fair weather the four day of April we fall with land again in thirty four degree and forty minute then we lie drive to and again in the sea with contrary wind and in sight of the shore so that we be twice within three or four league of the cape of Bona esperanza yet can not possible get about thus we lie drive to and again in the sea and in sight of the shore until the nineteen day of April they double the cape of Bona esperanza and then it please God that we double the foresay cape of Bona esperanza to our no little comfort be in great despair before and fear our winter at Mosambique which be a common thing among the portugal the seven and twenty of April we pail the tropic of Capricorn and the nine day of may we come to a anchor at the island of saint Helena which stand in fifteen degree of southerly latitude where we stay until the fifteen of the say month in water and then we weigh and direct our course for the pass of the equinoctial and the second of june we pass the same the six and twenty of the say month we pass the tropic of cancer with the wind at north-east which the portugal call the general wind and the sixteenth of july we pass by the westerly land by judgement of the pilot in the carrack be in the latitude of forty degree and odd minute to the north-ward we not see any land since our departure from saint Helena so praise be God the three day of August we make the land of Portugal the three of August they arrive at Lisbon 1610. be not above two league of the rock to our no little comfort and the same day we come to a anchor in the road of caskalle i the same day embark myself in a boat and go ashore and so escape the hand of the portugal I remain in Lisbon secret until the thirteen day of the say month and then I embark myself in a ship of London with master steed which be thither find and the same day we weigh anchor in the bay of wayer there be a boat full of portugal to have take the ship and so to have carry we ashore have have intelligence of our departure but we set sail put forth to sea and escape the danger and praise be God arrive at our long desire home the seventeen day of September 1610. it be two year and six month since our departure out of England @. 2 the report of WILLIAM NICOLS a mariner in the ascension which travel from Bramport by land to Masulipatan write from his mouth at Bantam by HENRY moris sept. 12. 1612. the former and great part be the same in substance with that of t. JONES and therefore omit the company depart from our general not able to provide for they and leave the rest to stay by he be very sick some go to one place and some to another and some back again for surat the company divide themselves and I myself be one of they that be willing to take the best course for myself that I can I tell they I will travel god-willing to Masulipatan for I know there be a holland factory there as I have hear at surat before we come from thence I can not find any Christian to travel over land with i and inquire at Bramport if there be any that will travel to Masulipatan I meet with company which be travel that way but it be such company that few englishman will travel with they for they be three jew but necessity have no law after I have agree to travel with they I think if I travel with any money the dog will cut my throat w. Nichols travel to Masulipatan so I make away with all my money and attire myself in the habit of a Turk and take my journey with those dog without any penny of money in my purse and travel with they four month have nothing to eat but only such food as the jew give i and many time when I be hungry they will give i no meat so that I be enforce to eat such meat as they give their camel and no better and glad I can get it nay sometime I be infor to be in fee with the camel keeper to give i a little in this miserable case I travel with these dog four month sometime they will say come let we cut this dog throat and afterward open his belly for he have eat his gold then will have cut my throat but the three be a honest dog for he will not consent unto it so with many a weary journey and hungry belly he arrive at Masulipatan and be kind entreat at the hollander house after a long and dangerous travel we come safe unto Masulipatan where I present discharge myself from these cruel dog and come unto the dutch house where the captain use i very kind and give i clothes and meat and drink five month before any ship come there at length there come three ship to Masulipatan the one call the hay the other the sun and the three be a frigate which they have take in the straits of malacca and the sun and the frigate be find for Bantam I entreat the master to grant i passage and I will labour for my passage who tell i very kind that he will not only give i passage but will also give i wage for the which I give he great thanks and so come aboard not long after we set sail from thence and come to Bantam the six day of September he arrive at Bantam the 6. of sept. 1610. 1610. being Thursday and come present to the english house with joyful heart 1610. in my travel with the three jew overland these fair town I pass which I bear in mind for I can neither write nor read first after I come from Bramport I come to jevaport from thence to huidare from thence to golacaude and so to Masulipatania @. 3 the unhappy voyage of the vice-admiral the union outward find till she arrive at Priaman reporee by a letter which master SAMVE^ Bradshaw send from Priaman by Humphrey BIDULPHE the eleven day of march 1609. write by the say henry moris at Bantam sept. the fourteen 1610. you have already hear of the passage of the two ship the ascension and the union from England to the cape Bona esperanza but after their departure out of the road of Saldania and of their lose one another in double of the cape as yet you have not hear therefore I think good to make some relation thereof as well as of the other and that true as from other man report I have hear and thus it be after they have lose one another by stormy weather in double of the cape the union in that storm spring her mainmast and in the midst of the storm they be enforce to fish it again by reason whereof they lose the company of their admiral and at last be without hope either to meet with ship or pinnace thereabouts consider that the storm continue they shape their course for the bay of s. Augustine be upon Madagascar they arrive at the b^y of s. Augustine in Madagascar where be arrive they go ashore and have good refresh and stay there twenty day be in good hope to have meet our admiral and the pinnace there but all their hope be frustrate then be out of all hope to have their company they set sail from thence and direct their course for zanzibar in hope to meet their general there where be arrive they go on shore and at first be kind entertain but at their next go ashore they lay in ambush the treachery of the people of zanzibar and as soon as they land sally out upon they and kill the purser present and one mariner and take one of their merchant prisoner yet by great chance they get off their boat and come aboard the name of they that be slay be Richard kenn Purser the mariner name I have forget but the merchant name that be take prisoner be Richard Wicham they put to sea about the month of February 1608. with the wind at north-east and northerly just against they as they shall go for Socotora now after they have spend much time at sea and little or nothing in the way and the most part of the man very much trouble with the scurvy the captain purpose and according bare up the helm for the north part of s. laurance they bear back again for s. Laurence determine to go for the bay of Antongil but they fall on the west side of the island intend to recover their almost-lost man there and spend the unprofitable monson upon which end of s. laurance they fall into a exceed great bay the great bay of Canquomorra or B^am^r^ which afterward they understand to be call by the country people Canquomorra a country very fruitful and pleasant to behold the very first view thereof give great content to all their man in general who no soon arrive in the bay but within short time have conference with the country people and at first they proffer they great kindness but after it prove to the contrary whereupon master rowles the captain and master Richard Reu chief merchant and jeffrey Carlel with three other which be attendant upon the captain adventure to go ashore unto the king and that make they the more venturous because diverse time before all the merchant have be ashore at the king palace in their Skiffe and long boat and speak with the king who proffer they great kindness and come aboard again as safe as if they have be in their own native country of England Samuel Bradshaw the captain and six other betray Samuel Bradshaw have be often employ about business unto the king yet it please God at this time the captain have some other occasion of business for he and so stay he aboard a happy turn for he for they no soon come ashore but they be betray by the country people but by the great providence of the almighty the boat escape and present come aboard and inform they of all that happen where they no soon have make know unto they this doleful news but present they see such abundance of prawe and great boat abundance of prawe and great boates. come out of the river unto they that it be admirable to behold the master speak unto the gunner to make the ordnance ready which be soon effect this fleet of infidel come row up unto their ship as though present they will have board they but by the diligence of the gunner and his mate he make they retire six boat of the enemy destroy by sink of some half dozen of their boat and they retire back again as fast as if they have be sheep chase by the wolf but before we make such massacre among they they come up in the face of our ordnance and we think very they will have take we all for the fight continue at least two hour very dangerous till we plague they so with our ordnance and then a fight for two house he account himself happy that first can clear himself and we continual send after they as far as the ordnance will reach after they be go from we in this first attempt we stay in the bay some fourteen day be in good hope to recover our lose man again they stay 14 day long in this Bay in which time we lose seven man more through a sudden disease which daunt we more than the malice of those infidel the man which die be they that wrought so lusty about the ordnance in the fight that within two day they be all throw overboard these cross come together and no hope to recover our lose man they think it folly to make any long stay there and therefore present make haste away and be not thorough water they think good to spend a little time in another place thereby but before they can dispatch they attempt against they the second time with a great multitude of boat and many of they great vessel a second attempt m^de by the enemy and so thick pester with man that it be wonderful but they like their first entertainment so well that they care not for come too near they the second time but go all on shore and place themselves to look upon the Ship then present perceive what their intend purpose be and fear some mischief in the night they weigh and stand in for the shore where all the infidel sit and give they a whole broad side for a farewell which fall among the thick of they and in their sight make such lane among they that they soon forsake their place and get out of their sight with as much speed as may be they depart from s. Laurence from thence they tack and stand off at sea leave behind they fourteen man seven betray and seven that di^d w^th sickness then be clear from those infidel they direct their course for Socotora but by some negligence for want of hull in betimes the wind take they short that they can not fetch it they fall upon the coast of Arabia but they fall more to the eastward upon the coast of Arabia which be about the four of june and the winter monson be come they can not nor dare go for Camba^a moreover upon that coast they can not find any good place to harbour themselves in until the winter be pass wherefore keep within sight of the coast four day sometime be in danger of the shore they think it but folly to neglect the time any long and therefore resolve upon some course to be take for the best performance of the voyage so the master call the best and most principal man in the ship and such as be best experience in those affair they present conclude altogether to go for Achen and be 2. day journey from agra what indigo be and the make thereof be but two month journey leave the way by lahor which be four month journey from agra to Biamy we spend two day travel Biamy be the chief place for indigo in all the east India where be twelve indigo mill it grow on small bush and bear a seed like a cabbage seed be cut down it lie on heap for half a year to rot and then by ox it be tread out from the stalk and afterward be ground very fine and then boil in fornace and so sort out into several sort the best indigo be there worth eight penny a pound from biamy we spend eight day
