force back by foul weather and west-wind the ten he depart from the west the thirteen he return have meet with the Hector in the straits of Sonda they be very weak their man for the most part touch with the scurvy the portugal of Damas have betray their boat at surat take nineteen of their man and nine thousand rial in cloth as it cost there item as they come for Bantam they take a small frigate of Collumba out of which they take eleven pack of cloth contain in all eighty three clothes thirteen piece pouling which be send for the land of Banda the sixteenth of December arrive a small ship from Holland by who we understand of two ship which they meet withal to the north of the cape Bona Speransa in thirty two degree they make they to be english ship but whether they be find they be not certain but the small ship bear the flag in the main-top this ship have be on her voyage eight month and ten day they refresh at one of the land of Comora call pulo Lamone where they have great store of beef and goat for old knife and tin spoon the two and twenty she set sail for Mallacca to their fleet which lie there to will they to give over their siege the three and twenty depart the dragon for England captain Gabriel Towerson the first of january 1608. our general William keeling set sail in the Hector for the land of Banda the seven arrive two ship and a pinnace of the fleming from Choromandell lade with cloth the which some part they have take and the rest buy they have take five prize one a carrack at Mosambique the fifteen of january 1608. depart the great sun and the two ship which come from Choromandell the three of February arrive admiral Willamson verhoofe with twelve sail of good ship from Mallaca the fourteen the admiral with seven ship depart for the molluccoe the nine of march the fleming cause a meeting at the court of all the pungavas to tell the king that they have receive letter from their king which do make mention of peace between they and the portugal a meeting at the court by the flem. procurement wherefore they think good to certify so much unto they to this end that if the portugal shall come thither under colour to trade with they and so set upon they for their country they can not take their part as aforetime they can have do by reason the king of Holland and Portugal be friend where at the javan fall all into a great laughter smoke they that their pretence be to strike fear into they of the Portugal doubt the king will if they come give they peaceable trade which will be the overthrow of the fleming the governor give they no answer but will they to take their course our house escape burn I be send for to the court. the twenty it please God to deliver we from a great danger for a chinese house next unto our Warehouse take fire and be burn down but we escape the one and twenty I be send for to the court by Pangran Areaumgalla the governor I go and carry with i a present which be one piece one Mallee Goobaer one piece morey one piece Mallayo Pintado one bandaleere one roll of match the which he accept very kind he tell i he have send for i hear that there be two man in chain in our house for debt and he will know by who order I keep they I tell he by the order of the king we have take they up and hope that he will not take they from i before I be satisfy my debt or some part and that it be due by they I show their bill he say he think they be indebt but that the king give we leave to chain they up he know to the contrary wherefore he will have they loose but with much entreaty I persuade that he give i leave to keep they till tanyomge which ought four hundred twenty rial and a half shall pay one hundred and bungoone which ought five hundred rial and one hundred sack of pepper shall pay twenty bag of pepper and one hundred rial in money according as he have before agree and give i his bill wherefore he send one of his slave home with i to tell the prisoner thereof will they to resolve and pay i the four and twenty I be send for to the court and the fleming he demand of the Fleming whether it be their country manner to take up a man for debt without tell of the king the Fleming say no whereupon he will i present to let they out the governors order I be send for to the court and will to deliver the chinese up clean forget his promise three day before the which I charge he with but all will not prevail wherefore he send one of the king slave and take they out of the house the which strict course I hold to be take against we by the instigation of the fleming wrought by lackmoye to the end we shall not trust the chinese so that by this course they must needs come to he and he be fit with all sort of commodity from the Fleming will whole overthrow our trade in respect we can trust but at hazard for there be no justice to be have the three and twenty of April 1609. here arrive a small pinnace of the fleming from Soocadanna and Ternata a pinnace of the fleming from Soocadana a pinnace of the fleming for Bemermassin by who we understand that admiral Paul vankerle be take at Ternata the one and twenty of May 1609. a pinnace of the fleming set sail for Bemermassin upon a league make between they and with purpose to search every creek and corner of the island for they have hear there be much gold there and bezoar the which be to be trade for with bead and other haberdasher-ware the six and twenty of August 1609. arrive captain William keeling from Banda have lade there twelve thousand four hundred eighty four cattee one half quarter of mace fifty nine thousand eight hundred forty six cattee of nutmeg which stand they in nine ten and eleven rial the Bahar the Cattee there weigh thirteen and a half of our english ounce the small Bahar mace be ten cattee or one hundred cattee of nutmeg and the great Bahar be one hundred cattee of mace or one thousand cattee of nutmeg so that if a man be indebt unto you ten cattee of mace and will give you one hundred cattee of nutmeg you can refuse it the four of October 1609. captain keeling set sail from Bantam have take in the rest of his lade which be four thousand nine hundred bag three cattee of pepper the Hector set sail from Bantam in the which ship call the Hector I come for England have be in the country four year nine month eleven day certain rule for the choice of sundry drug as also from whence they may be have as follow aloe be a wood so call by we but of the Mallayens it be call Garroo the best come from Syam and Cambaya also from sumatra Potannie Cauchauchene the best be that which be in large round stick and very massy of black colour intermix with ashe-coloured vein in taste somewhat bitter and odoriferous and be burn it become like unto pitch in bubble if a splinter thereof be lay upon a fire-coale for if it be good it will not leave fry till it be quite consume cast forth a most delectable odour Benjamin be a gum call by the Mallayens minnian the best sort come from Syam which be very pure clear and white with little streak of amber colour burrowse yield tyurall call in english Buris worth there a rial the Cattee and here ten shilling the pound it be keep in grease the other sort which be not altogether so white but be also very good come from sumatra and a three sort which come from Priaman and barrowse be very course like horsebread not vendible in England but well esteem in Bantam Civet the best be that which be of a deep yellow colour somewhat incline to the colour of gold not whitish for that be usual sophisticate with grease yet if it be new take it be natural whitish and will in continuance of time become of a yellowish colour musk there be three sort black brown and yellow of which the first be naught the second be good the last best which ought to be of colour like the best spikenard that be of a deep amber colour enclose with one only skin and not one over another as it be oftentimes to be see not over-moist which make it weighty but in a mean have some hair like bristle but not overmany clear of stone lead or other trash intermix and of so strong and fragrant a smell that to many it be offensive and be taste in the mouth it pierce the very brain with the scent and ought not oversoone to dissolve in the mouth nor yet to remain very long undissolue in any hand it must not be keep near to any sweet spice lest it lose the send bezoar there be here of two kind the one bring from the west the other from the east indies whereof the east India bezoar be worth double the price of the other the form of ^oth be diverse some round other long like date-stone other like pigeon egg some like the kidney of a young goat and other in form of a chestnut but all for the most part be ^l^nt at the end not pick and no less variety be also to be see in the colour for some be of light red which be a^ the (@) into Cambaya other of colour like honey many of a dark ash-colour like that of the civetcat but for the most part of a waterish-greene the east India bezoar consist of many peel and scale as it be artificial compact together in manner of the skin and peele of a onion each enclose other bright and splendent as if they be polish by art the one peel be break off the next be more splendent or bright than the former these peel be some thick some thin according to the largeness of the stone and the large the stone be the better for sale this be a certain way to make trial of bezoar take the direct weight of the stone than put he into water and let it stand for the space of four hour then see if he be not crack wipe it dry and weigh it again if it weigh never so small a matter more than he do at the first then build upon it it be not good thus have I prove myself many time in Bantam and have have diverse turn to chalk with a little stick in the middle which have weigh a tail which be two ounce the most counterfeit come from Soocodanna which be upon Burneo these name in the margin be the place from whence they may be have amber there be hereof if you regard the colour many sort as black white brown and gray of all which the black be usual the base and the gray the best of which choose what be best cleanse from filth or dross pure of itself of colour incline to a white and of a ash-colour intermix with vein some ash-colour other whitish be put into a bowl of water it ought to float aloft the which although some which be sophisticate may do yet this be (@) that none which be pure will sink in the water the great quantity come from Mosambique and Sofala of all the chief and principal continue most part of the town have be burn but the wind fall variable south-easter and in the end calm yet notwithstanding forty house be burn to the ground and have not our english man bestir themselves lusty many more house have go to wrack for the fire take hold three or four time on the other side the street where our english house be but they still put it out and be very much commend of the king and all other in general the old king foin come on horseback to our door and wish we to put all thing into the gadonge and daub up the door and then it be out of danger captain brower and some of his people come very kind to the english house to have assist we by land or water if need have be it can certain be know how this fire begin but there be speech among the japan that there will be a great fire than any of these it be tell they by the devil and their conjurer God grant it be not do by some villainous ill mind people think to rob and steal what they can lay hold on in time of such trouble and confusion the twenty in the morning I go to the dutch house to visit captain brower and to give he thanks for his friendly visitation and assistance the last night and towards night Harnando the Spaniard and Edward mark return from but can not come to sight of any of our runaway yet it be certain that they be in and a Portugal or Spaniard a great man in about sea-matter tell Edward mark that we shall have none of these man back but to the contrary if all the rest will come and leave the ship empty they will give they entertainment yea and that which be more if they will bring away the ship and all they shall be the more welcome the japan which the king send to accompany Edward mark and Harnando and to look out our people will not let Edward mark budge out a door in the space of one night and half a day after they be arrive there at he go abroad himself and the Spaniard Harnando lie at another place so I doubt some legerdy-maine betwixt they two and be now out of all hope to have any of our people come back I blame the jesuit and the old king like well of my speech and tell i he will take such order hereafter that none of our people shall be carry to except they steal away our ship-boat as the other do of which I advise the master master james Foster and so a edict be set out that no man shall carry or convey away any of our people without make it know unto i and tell the king thereof the three and twenty I be give to understand of a great pagan feast that be to be perform this day and that both the king with all the rest of the nobility accompany with diverse stranger solemn feast the manner thereof meet together at a summer-house set up before the great pagoda to see a horse-race I think there be not so few as three thousand person assemble together as I esteem in view of they every nobleman go on horseback to the place accompany with a ro^t o^ slave some with p^kes some with smallshot and other with bow and arrow the pike-man be place on the one side of the street and the shot and archer on the other the midst of the street be leave void to run the race and right before the summer-house where the king and noble sit be a round buckler of straw hang against the wall at which the archer on horseback run a full career discharge their arrow both in the street and summer-house where the noble sit that neither the present which we send nor we can have entrance and so we pass along the street behold all and return another way to the english house and late at night zanzebar wife brother come to the english house and bring i a present of a haunch of venison and a basket of orange zanzebar himself do accompany he and about ten of the clock in the night the captain Chinesa our landlord come and knock at the door tell i that the king have give express command that every house shall have a tub of water ready on the top of their house for that the devil have say the town shall be burn this night the devil again a liar if the knave belie not their master yet he prove a liar but for all that we get a great tub of water on the top of our house which hold twen^ie bucket of water and man do run up and down the street all night bid every one look to their fire that it be strange and fearful to hear they the four and twenty this report of burn the town be still current and every one make provision to prevent it I make ready fifteen bucket which cost six condrin a piece and fill they full of water and hang they up in the yard and set another great tub by they full of water beside that w^ich stand on the top of the house and give order to make a couple of ladder to carry water to the top of the house and have former provide nine empty wine-barrel full of temper clay to daub up our gad^nge door if need shall require God defend we from any such necessity three or four man do run up and down the stre^tes all night make a horrible noise that every one shall have a care thereof that it be bot^ strange and fearful to hear they the five and twenty the captain Chinesa our landlord be sick send for a piece of pork which I send he and present follow after myself to visit he and carry he a small bottle of spanish wine and while I be there Semedone and our guardian father in law come likewise to visit he the king send i word by miguell our jurebasso that he have a bad opinion of Harnando ximenes our Spaniard and that he go about to have run away when he be last at but that I know be not so for he have free liberty to go when he will without run away another complaint be also make of he that he be a common gamester and have bring on diverse to play and get their money which report I do rather believe then the other and I find by experience these people be no friend neither of Spaniard nor Portugal and love they of the worse because they love they so well and I have almost forget to note down a shame to belie the devil so often that the night pass ill dispose people have think to have fire the town in three place and in one place set a house on fire but it be soon put out and no hurt do but the party that do it be not find out of doubt it be nothing but a villainy of these conjurer and other base people which be give to the spoil hope to get or steal away something when the town be on fire the six and twenty master Melsham be very sick zanzebar come to visit he and put he in mind to take the physic of this country bonze physician and that it will present stop his flax and bring a bonze or doctor with he to administer it master Melsham be very desirous to take it but that first our chirurgeon shall see it and so he give he two pill yesterday two in the night and two in the morning with certain other feed but for aught I can see it do he no good at all God send he his health all our waste-clothe pendant brass shiver and other matter be send aboard and the ship put in order to receive the general another house be set on fire the night pass by villain but soon put king themselves with the great nobleman and prince their play in which the king themselves be author with their great noble the matter be of the valiant deed of their ancestor from the begin of their kingdom or commonwealth until this present with much mirth mix among to give the common people content the audience be grea^ for no house in town but bring a present nor no village nor place under their dominion but do the like and be spectator and the king themselves do see that every one both great and small do eat and drink before they depart their act music and sing as also their poetry be very harsh to we yet they keep due time both with hand and foot their music be little taber make great at both end their act song and music and small in the midst like to a hourglass they beat on the end with one hand and strain the cord which go about it with the other which make it to sound great or small as they listen according their voice with it one play on a phife or flute but all harsh and not pleasant to our hear yet I never see play wherein I note so much for I see their policy be great in do thereof and quite contrary to our comedy in Christendom we be but dumb show and this the truth itself act by the king themselves to keep in perpetual remembrance their affair the king do not send for the fleming and therefore I account it a great grace for we at our return to the english house I find three or four fleming there one of they be in a japan habit cushma corea and come from a place call cushma within sight of corea I understand they sell pepper and other commodity there and I think have some secret trade into corea or else be very likely to have I hope if they do well we can do amiss m. Adam be the man that put they forward unto it and no doubt will be as forward for the good of his own country as for stranger Hernando ximenes be with captain brower and see the two man which come from cushma dutch jealousy and do but ask he from whence they come whereat captain brower be angry tell he he will give he no account thereof and towards night I understand that two spaniard be come from and lodge at zanzibar and send for our jurebassa to come to they but I will not let he go so soon after zanzibar and they come to the english house the one of they be Andres Bulgaryn the genowe which pass by this place the other day and the other be call benito de palais and be pilot Maior of the spanish ship which be cast away on the coast of japan and be the same man which come from to visit m. Adams at his be here they tell i they be come of purpose to visit their friend namely myself first of all with many other word of compliment and then enter into speech of our fugitive say it be not the father as they call they which keep our people secret or go about to convey they away but rather they of themselves bad people who they report to be very bad people in fine I stand in doubt that these fellow be come of purpose to inveigle more of our people to do as the other have do and thereof advise the master to have a care both to ship and boat as also to take notice of any such as go about to keep they company for that it be good to doubt the worst for the best will save itself November 1. 1613. the first of November at night two house be set on fire on the other side the water but fire be soon put out but the villain that do it can not be find I send m. Foster the master a letter advise he to take care of ship and boat as also to look unto the behaviour of our people for that I doubt these two spaniard be but come as spy to see what we do and to entice some other of our people to do as the former do also I advise he how I understand the say spaniard do pretend to invite he to dinner this day but I wish he to take heed they give he not a Hig^ he return i answer that he esteem they such as I take they for and therefore will have a care to the main chance but soon after he come ashore and the spaniard come to the english house and with much entreaty get m. villain get into a poor widow house think to have rob she but she make a outcry he flee up into the wood over against the english house where the pagoda be and soon after the wood be beset round about the pagoda be the idol or idol-temple or both with above five hundred man but the thief can not be find at night as we be go to bed there be a outcry on a sudden that thief be on the top of our house set it on fire but our ladder be ready rear both myself and other be not long a go up but find nothing but that all our neighbour house be people on the top on a sudden as well as we and it be to be think it be nothing but a false lar^m give of purpose to see how every one will be find in a readiness yet at that very instant there be a house set on fire but soon quench it be a good way from our english house the night past three house be set on fire in diverse part of the town but all put out at beginning so that no hurt be do so now order be give to take notice in every house what people be in they whether stranger or other order to prevent fire-knave and night-crye and such as be find to be suspect be to be banish out of the country and gate or bar make to shut up the passage or end of street and watch set in diverse place without cry and make a noise up and down street in the night as have be for a time heretofore without either form or fashion yet notwithstanding all this a villain about ten a clock in the night set a house on fire near unto the pagoda over against our english house but he be espy by the watch who pursue he with all speed but he get into the wood above the pag^d which forthwith be beset round about with above five hundred arm man and the old king foin come in person with many other noble man assist in the pursuit yet I very think the villain do run up and down among the rest cry keep thief as well as the best the four the night pass there be fire put in diverse place more one in the town and a other in the country beside the house near we as I say before order be now give to have secret watch in diverse part of the town every night and no man to go out in the night except upon urgent occasion and then to have a light before they to the end they may be see if this decorum be due keep our house burner will play least in sight I tell the king and other hereof above a week past and now it be put in execution the five this morning I receive two letter the one from Domingo Francisco the spanish ambassador date in five day past and the other from George the Portugal the ambassador go over land from thence for and send his servant with the wherein the japonian affair and various occurrent for diverse year be express the copy of a letter send by the emperor of japan unto the king of Holland by the ship call the red lion with arrow which arrive in the texel the two and twenty of july 1610. i emperor and king of japan wish to the king of Holland who have send from so far country to visit i greeting I rejoice great in your writing and send unto i and wish that our country be near the one to the other whereby we may continue and increase the friendship begin betwixt we through your majesty presence who I imagine in conceit to see in respect I be unknown unto your majesty and that your love towards i be manifest through your liberality in honour i with four present whereof though I have no need yet come in your name I receive they in great worth and hold they in good esteem and further whereas the hollander your majesty subject desire to trade with their ship in my country which be of little value and small and to traffic with my subject and desire to have their abide near unto my court whereby in person I may help and assist they which can be as now through the inconveniency of the country yet notwithstanding I will not neglect as already I have be to be careful of they and to give in charge to all my governor and subject that in what place and haven in what part soever they shall arrive they shall show they all favour and friendship to their person ship and merchandise wherein your majesty or your subject need not to doubt or fear aught to the contrary for they may come as free as if they come into your majesty own haven and country and so may remain in my country to trade and the friendship begin betwixt i and my subject with you shall never be impair on my behalf but augment and increase I be partly ashamed that your majesty who name and renown through your valorous deed be spread throughout the whole world shall cause your subject to come from so far country into a country so unfitting as this be to visit i and to offer unto i such friendship as I have not deserve but consider that your affection have be the cause thereof I can not but friendly entertain your subject and yield to their request whereof this shall serve for a testimony that they in all place country and land under my obedience may trade and traffic and build house serviceable and needful for their trade and merchandize where they may trade without any hindrance at their pleasure aswell in time to come as for the present so that no man shall do they any wrong and I will maintain and defend they as my own subject I promise likewise that the person which I understand shall be leave here shall now and at all time be hold as recommend unto i and in all thing to favour they whereby your majesty shall find we as your friend and neighbour for other matter pass betwixt i and your majesty servant which will be too long here to repeat I refer myself unto they Firando in japan the ten of December 1614 to this day I have not have time to perfe up my old book of account by mean of the dispatch away our people some to one place some to another and then the new build of our house and after that the buy of a juncke trade at Syam and repair of she which be now ready to depart for Syam and have be any time this ten day ride at a anchor at Cochi a league from Firando where your ship ride at your departure from hence expect but affair wind to set forward on her voyage she be call the sea adventure be about some two hundred ton in who master Adams go for master and master wickham and Edward sayer for merchant m. peacock slay in Cochinchina by mean of the death of master peacock slay in Cochinchina and likelihood of cast away Walter Carwaden return back from thence for to this hour we have no news of he ^or the juncke they go in as I have at large advise the worshipful company jesuite banish etc. since your departure from hence the emperor have banish all jesuit priest friar and nun out of japan and pull down and burn all their church and monastery ship they away some for Amacau in China and the rest for manillias Foyne same the old king of Firando be dead Foyne same dead civil war in fidaia-same the young prince son to tico-same who have fortify himself strong in his castle or fortress of osak^y have eighty thousand or a hundred thousand man run away and banish man mall-content effect hope of trade in China for three ship a year to come and go to a place near Lanquin to which place we may go from hence in three or four day if the wind be good I have write hereof at large to the worshipful company as the like to my lord treasurer some little sickness I have have but now I praise God it be past master wickham master Eton master Nealson and master Edward sayer have all four be very sick but now well recover all except master Eton who be trouble with the flux and a tertian ague God send he his health for I can too much praise that man for his diligence and pain take in the worshipful company affair jacob speck who be think to be cast away in go from hence to the Moluccas be now return to Firando captain of a great ship call the Zelandia with a little pinnace call the jaccatra the cause of his so long miss be for that the ship wherein he go from hence pass to the eastward of the the same way we come yet by current and contrary wind as they say they can not fetch the Moluccas but be drive to the westward of the island celebe and so pass round about it through the straits of Desalon and so back to the Moluccas etc. the chinaes do much complain of the hollander rob and pilfer their junck for as they say they have rifle and take seven the emperor of japan have take some distaste against the hollander for he refuse a present they late send up to he and will not speak to they which bring it hollander distaste by chineis and japan Portugall not accept as he do the like by another present the portugal send he who come in the great ship from Amacau this year to he refuse both the present as also to speak to they which bring it you think at your be here that if any other ship come out of England we may sell our good without carry up any present to the emperor but now I find it to be otherwise for every ship which come in must carry a present to the emperor as a custom neither can we set out any juncke present a custom for every ship without procure the yearly licence of the emperor otherwise no japan mariner dare go out of japan upon pain of death only our own ship from England may come in and go out again when they will and no man gainsay it we can yet by any mean get trade from tushma into corea neither have they of tushma any other privilege but to enter unto one little town or fortress and in pain of death not to go without the wall thereof to the landward and yet the king of tushma be no subject to the emperor of japan we can vent nothing but pepper at tushma and yet no great quantity of that and the weight be much big than that of japan but sell at a better rate I be give to understand that up in the country of corea they have great city and betwixt that and the sea mighty bog corea bogges and sail wagon so that no man can travel on horseback nor very hardly on foot but for remedy against that they have great wagon or cart which go upon broad or flat wheel under sail as ship do so that observe monsons they transport their good too and fro in these sail wagon they have damask satin taffeta and other silk stuff make there as well as in China it be say that ticus-same otherwise call the decease emperor do pretend to have convey a great army of soldier in these sail wagon to have assault the emperor of China on a sudden in his great city of Paquin Paquin where he be ordinary resident but he be prevent by a corean nobleman who poison himself to poison the emperor and other great man of japan which be the occasion the japan have lose that which some two and twenty year pass they have get possession of in corea james Turner the fiddle youth leave a wench with child here but the whore the mother kill it so soon as it be bear although I give she two tay in plate before to nourish it because she shall not kill it it be a ordinary thing here master Foster the master whistle and chain be find and master Adams have it and will be answerable unto he for it I do think to have send you a japan almanac in another letter to the same effect as this date the five and twenty and send by sea-aduenture by way of Syam but forget to put it in yet now come here enclose I pray you let this letter suffice to master George Sa^is your brother and the rest of my love friend and with hearty commendation in general I leave you all to the holy protection of the almighty rest always your ever love friend at command richard cock to the worshipful THOMAS Wilson esquire at his house at the britaine-burse at the strand give these sir my last unto you be of the first of December 1613. date in the matter of moment to advise you of more than I have touch in another letter to my good lord treasurer the hollander give it out here that it be very likely our east India company of England and that of their commander allege that all the benefit which happen either by reprisal or conquest be for the state and winthebber as they call they so that what will come of this in the end be hard to judge but the king keep his residence in the bottom of the bay and be call by the moor or captain Caran caran caran he have other petty king under he whereof one call captain pinto a wretched old man dwell at a path other wear it jagged in tuft other in other foolish form but the woman shave all close to the flesh their town consist of thirty or forty house all cluster together yet each have his own cover about the wall yet most about their bed betwixt they and the wall their other furniture be two or three pot of earth to keep water in and to boil such meat as they can get a gourd or two to fetch for the settle of trade and factory in the city of surat Cambaya Amadavar Goga or in any other part or part of this country within the great mogul dominion witness under our hand and seal the one and twenty of October 1612. 1 that all which concern sir Henry Middleton be remit acquit and clear to we that they shall never make seizure stoppage nor stay of our good ware and merchandize to satisfy for the same 2 that they shall procure from their king the great mogoll at their proper cost his grant and confirmation of all the article of agreement under the great seal of his land and shall deliver the same unto we for our security and certainty of perpetual amity commerce and deal with they within forty day after the seal hereof 3 that it shall be lawful for the king of England to keep and continue his ambassador at the court of the great mogoll during the time of the say peace and commerce there to compound and end all such great and weighty question as may any way tend to the breach of the say peace 4 that at all time upon the arrival of our ship in the road of Swally there shall be proclamation in the city of surat three several day together that it shall be free for the country people of all sort to come down to the water side there to have free trade deal and commerce with we 5 that all english commodity shall pay custom according to the value or price that it bear at the time that it be put into the customhouse after the rate of three and a half the hundred 6 that all petty and pedler wear be free of custom provide that it exceed not in value ten rial of eight 7 that we shall have ten for our Manuda carry from the water side to surat and after the same rate back again and for cart we be to repair to the Moccadam of Swally to send for surat and at surat to repair to the broker for cart down again 8 that if any of our man die in those part that then neither the king nor governor nor under officer shall make title or challenge to any thing that to the dead belong nor demand fee nor any kind of tax nor custom 9 that if all our man die here in these part between the time of the come of our ship that then by some office thereto appoint just and true inventory notice and knowledge be take of all such money good jewel provision apparel and what else to our nation belong and the same shall safe preserve and keep and deliver to the general captain or merchant of the first ship that shall after here arrive and to receive a discharge from the general captain or merchant to who such good and money shall be deliver 10 that they secure our man and good upon the land redeem all such both good and man as shall happen to be take upon the land by the portugal and shall deliver both man and good again to we free of all charge or the value of our good and man instant 11 that as in all kingdom there be some rebel and disobedient subject so in our nation there may be some pirate and sea-rover which may happen to come into these part and here may rob and steal if any such shall happen then will not we by our trade and factory here be liable or answerable for such good so take but will aid they with our best mean that be so grieve by justice to our king for redress and restitution unto they 11 that all such provision of victual as shall be spend during the time that our ship shall remain here in the road of surat and Swally shall be free of custom provide it do not amount unto above a thousand dollar in money 13 that in all question of wrong and injury that shall be offer unto we and to our nation that we do receive from the judge and those that be in authority present and speedy justice according to the quality of our complaint and wrong be do we and that by delay we be not put off and weary either by time or charge the fourteen I land the present for the great mogul and bring it to the tent of the governor of Amadavar who take notice of the particular also of our king letter to their king to advertise their king thereof which do I return the present to my ship again according to agreement with the say governor for I have tell he that unless their king will confirm the article conclude on and likewise write our king a letter I will not deliver the present nor our king letter for if he refuse so to do than be he not a friend but a enemy and to the enemy of my king I neither have letter nor present also the same day to Sinde as surat but there be more thieve which the mogoll seek to prevent inhabitant of sinda be most razbootche banians and boloche in city and great town razbootch the governor be mogul the country people be rude naked from the waist upward with turban contrary to the mogoll fashion their arm sword buckler and lance their buckler great in fashion of a beehive in which they will give their camel drink and horse provender their horse good swift strong which they ride unshod most desperate they back they at twelve month old the mogoll say the razbootch know as well to die as any in the world they eat no beef nor buffoll but pray to they the banians kill nothing Banian there be thirty and odd several cast of these that differ something in religion and may not eat with each other but all burn their dead when the husband die the wife shave her head and wear her jewel no more so continue till death funeral burn of the rasbut wife when the rasbut die his wife accompany his body go to be burn in her best array accompany with her friend and kindred and music and the fire be make at the place appoint compass the same twice or thrice bewail first her husband death and then rejoice that she shall now live with he again after which embrace her friend she last sit down on the top of the pile and dry stick take her husband head in her lap and b^ds they put fire which do her friend throw oil and other sweet perfume on she she endure the fire with admirable patience loose and not find I have see many the first in surat the woman but ten year old and a virgin he a soldier slay in war from whence his clothes and turban be bring home she will needs burn with his clothes the governor forbid she which she take grievous bid they put to fire present her husband be a great way before which they dare not till her kindred entreat with a present give the governors licence to her exceed joy the husband kindred never force this but the woman hold it a disgrace else to their family they may choose but few do but then must shave their hair and break their jewel and thenceforth be not suffer to eat drink sleep or company with any body and so continue till death if after purpose to burn they leap out of the fire her father and mother will bind she and throw she in and burn she perforce but this weakness be seldom the boloche be of Mahomet religion they deal much in camel boloche most of they robber by land and on the river murder such as they rob when I be in sinda they take a boat with seven italian one Portugal Friar the rest slay in fight this be rip by they for Gold there be very honest of they in guzerate and about agra banian marriage be make at the age of three year and under sometime they make mutual promise if two pregnant woman prove to have one a male the other a female banian marriage but always one of their own cast and religion and of the same trade as a barber etc. when they be three or four year old they make a great feast set the two thus espouse on horseback a man behind each to hold they in their best clothes accompany with the braman or priest and many other according to their state and so lead they up and down the city where they dwell and then to the pagoda or church and after ceremony there do come home continue certain day feast as they be able be ten year old they lie together of which they give this reason not to leave they wifeless if their parent die and leave they parentlesse their braman keep their pagoda and have alm or tithe esteem marvelous holy marry and follow occupation good workman apt to learn any pattern they eat but once a day and wash before and after meat all their body as also after urine or stool John mild^all * * see before his letter a Englishman have be employ with three English young man which he poison in Persia to make himself master of the good but he be likewise poison yet by preservative live many month after but swell exceed and so come to agra with the value of twenty thousand dollar tither therefore I go may the four 1614 from surat come to Bramport where sultan perue lie situate in a plain the river of surat run by in a great breadth have a large castle hence to don Robert Shirley the king of persian ambassador who desire grant of trade in this port be under my government which willing I will have grant but only for prejudicial inconvenience ensue for they bring not merchandise sit in quantity to begin such trade neither the portugal by who trade at present I reap benefit will consent thereto threaten to be go if I do receive the english nation so that thereby I shall have be leave destitute of all trade whereof those sum of money do arise yearly which I be find to pay unto the king majesty and in default therein I shall put in hazard his highness displeasure to my utter overthrow and undo yet notwithstanding for the love I owe unto the king of Persia by who ambassador I be request and the affection I bear unto the english nation together with his business with the mogoll as also the willingness of Arah Manewardus to entertain we at this port which opportunity be let slip we shall never obtain the like his lordship protest and vow to do his take boat there flock about we many of the country people also there come down to we about a dozen of the envious portugal who begin to talk with we in dutch as before demand of we many frivolous question which when I have answer I speak in their own language because the banians which be there present may understand and tell they that they be a shameless and lie people in spread of so many devise scandal and slanderous report of our nation unto who they know themselves much inferior in many respect and that they do it only in malicious policy because they will not have we to trade in the indies as well as they also I tell they that if they do not contain themselves within the compass of better peace reform themselves hereafter both in their saying and do they shall be all root out of the indies and a more honest and royal nation place in their room then one of the chief of they single out himself and answer thus that they have enemy too many already and therefore they desire no more and as for scandalous speech they do not deny be urge thereunto for not long pass off from surat they have a ship take by english man as they suppose to which I answer they that it may be rather the hollander so they conclude in the end very pliant and sociable wish that we may trade in all part of the indies with they and they with we like neighbour and friend and that there be some agreement make betwixt our king and they for the bring to pass thereof thus they take their leaf of we in very kind manner we part the six we arrive aboard our ship again where it be agree upon that master Salbanck shall go as aforesaid with the ambassador for agra wherefore he fit himself think to have go ashore the next day and in the mean time the captain send the purser and his man to buy fresh victual and provision for the sea who when they come to the city be by the governor present turn back again as they go and express command by proclamation upon pain of death the country people shall bring no more english man ashore these sudden and strange alteration make we much to marvel for we can never know the certainty whereupon it grow or what shall be the cause all the time of our way to our ship we see our friend the malabar which have desire to go with we not attempt to come forth we hasten to get up our anchor and to set sail to proceed on our journey yet see come in from the westward another fleet of Portugal frigate I be willing to show my best in the view of the country people to hinder their come into the river of surat their departure which be nothing for that there be room enough for they to pass by we every way out of the reach of our shot yet we shoot at the near of they without hope to shoot near they but only to show our good will and for encouragement to our friend on land as also for those which go alongst the coast as I esteem to give knowledge to the galleon of our come that they may report also that we shoot at their fellow go to surat that they may also expect that we care the less for their great strength in our passage this night we have diverse flaw of unconstant wind for which we come to anchor for a while afterward see it blow steady though faint we set sail continue our course south by east alongst the shore the enemy force descry at that time the daylight begin to discover to we all thing near we we descry between we and the shore our enemy force of galleon and two galley all come to sail present after they see we and stand after we with a faint gale we stand somewhat without our course with all our sail partly to gain time to make ourselves in perfect readiness to fight partly to refresh my people that have take much pain the night past as also the further I draw they off the coast the further they will be from fresh supply to be send they but ere long the tide of flood be come and little wind to hold our own we come to a anchor while the enemy rest his hope in the wind keep long under sail to his great disadvantage but I not take it for a error in they but of purpose to do we more harm it bring i into a new and great doubt which draw all my power to devise how to prevent this be that now we be at sea they mean to return to surat with all their strength and there to work their will on our friend and good which I have no mean to prevent but by follow they know they dare not unarm nor unfurnish their ship while I be in sight of they but the time now grow so late that I doubt by the most haste that I can make I shall hardly get off the coast before the foul weather come which put i into some hope that the viceroy be so great a soldier and so discreet a gentleman will not expose himself his people and ship to such great peril as the hasten winter do threaten while these th^ngs float in my mind the tide of flood be spend and time to work if we make use of the ebb we to my great content see the viceroy his fleet stand towards we with a fresh gale of wind we likewise set sail and stand away our own course before he all that tide and so spend the night to the best advantage partly by sail and partly by stop the five in the morning we see the enemy have get but little ground of we this day also we spend as before in ride and sail as time serve to our best advantage and for that the Hector go best and the hope logloaden worst I send to the Hector to take in her boat and to prepare for the hope I send to the hope to give direction to hasten to the Hector to be tow and to the end she shall have nothing to hinder she I have her boat to tow at my stern and so spend the night work for the best the wind fresh we have no cause to anchor this night the viceroy ship get much ground of we by this I be get well off from the shore and also a end to the southwards and by his work I recover some assurance to my conceit that these force will not this year annoy surat and for my business for encounter the enemy I have by good leisure well consider how to contrive it and withal I have consider of the case of either and the difference between the viceroy and i I mean in our several satisfaction and content my come hither be by the authority of my king and to follow the design of my employer which be in merchant ship fit for defence wise and sober course and to endeavour by honest commerce without strive to injury any which God have of his tender mercy and bountiful blessing so assist i that we have perform beyond my former conceit and in most thing hitherto God have grant i my heart desire and be now in a good way upon my way with the same with which without further tempt of God or presume of god continue mercy in further deliverance if I by pride swerve from what be just and before he to be allow who mercy have be free and without any cause in i for his own name sake therefore I hold it fit to proceed sober and attend upon the enemy attempt yet not in base manner but in a warlike sort on the other side the unhappy viceroy a famous valiant man therefore now send by his master the king of Spain with ship the principal of India with man all the gallant and principal braggart of those near part of India what to do thankful consideration of god assist our equity and punish the Portugal pride not only to disturb or intercept the peaceable and quiet trade of the english with the subject of the mogul a great king in his own country but to take or burn they so little regard be have to the effusion of christian blood never look towards the judgement of God nor remember that as man do to other they must expect to be do to this captain be furnish with abundance of all thing the country may yield and want nothing but a upright cause fit for God to favour he come to the place where he find what he seek four poor merchant ship a few man and many of they sick and dead and those braggart measure our mind by their own think we will never stand out against so powerful a force as they esteem they have and the conceit of that set those coxcomb a mad to be do mischief to increase their pride which they entitle honour I see the difference and the cause I have to pray to God my only refuge who it please to grant the request of i his poor and unworthy servant in consideration whereof I put forward the business and as it be bait my hook and the fish present run thereat as aforesaid they come three ship and thirty or forty frigate as I imagine with a veaze lay the hope aboard with the flower of all their gallant where by the hand of God in their amaze carriage they receive such a blow as few and they by their extraordinary chance escape with safety and the three ship burn thus it please God to cross their first attempt and never after though they beleaguer we round about by sea with all their sort of ship for many day together our people still in action and half tire with continual labour some receive in good yet bless be God they can never get the advantage to win from we the vallewe of a louse unless our bullet which we lend they his fire-boat fail and nothing prosper and once in four and twenty hour I send he a defiance for many day together to try his temper all which must needs lie heavy on the stomach of a gentleman of so great courage I esteem now he will hazard much to recover some of his honour former lose but crave pardon for this my digression I will now return and proceed with my former business wherefore the six in the morning betimes I send for my master and let he know that my purpose be that when the viceroy shall come up near with we that we will all at once cast about with he and charge he first on the sudden to strike a unexpected terror in the heart of his people who now be brag see we go away before they and to that end I now go aboard every ship to give they all direction and so that it grow to be midday near which time my ship which I leave far asterne for my better come aboard strike sail whereat as we imagine the viceroy see the admiral strike her sail to fall a stern may take it of purpose to stay for he in contempt he with his consort bear up with the shore and give over the hope of their fortune by further follow of we which course I like very well since he be so patient for there be nothing under his foot that can make amends for the loss of the worst man finger I have beside I wish no occasion to fight r^sh fight be ^ather humour than honour for that which I have already pay for I be already possess on and I be so far from the humour to fight for honour unless for the honour of my king or country that I have rather save the life or life of one of and in the wind unsavoury a dozen yard off filch treacherous unworthy so good a land which in likelihood with culture will be very fertile the six of August we have sight of saint Laurence this night A.D. 1615. chap. 14 memorial of a voyage wherein be employ three ship the samaritan Thomas and Thomasine 1614 write by * * the journal have not the author name but I find he thus name by captain payton as chief at tecoo Soldania in thirty three degree fifty minute south JOHN milward merchant who go in the Thomas the ten of may 1614 we anchor at gore-end the three of October in the bay of Soldania where we buy one hundred and forty sheep and ten ox and more may have do these people be most miserable destitute of religion in any kind so far as we can perceive and of all civility their speech a chatter rather then language naked save a short cloak of skin on their shoulder and a fox-skinne before their privity have but one stone natural or ceremonious I know not eat that which dog will hardly digest they demand unreasonable for their cattle which we think proceed from cory who have be in England and as we suppose acquaint they with our little esteem of iron and copper ask piece as big as their cloak and have for their cattle skillet basin and scummer one seem to be chief who the general kind entertain in his tent and we after that buy more free their sheep like our goat with small horn their ox large than we the flesh white like our mutton the fat yellow as the yolk of a egg wild and of one stone most of they like themselves October be with they as April with we the weather temperate but hot and parch at noon the air wholesome our man present recover some desperate sick they of the scurvy use a red Berry as big as a goose-berry the twenty of December the general cause the master and masters-mate to come aboard the copy of this voyage be so hurt with wet that I can not in some place read it and therefore have deliver it more imperfect they know not where they be trade wind suppose that we be shoot one hundred and fifty league more than reckon to the east in eighteen degree forty minute the nine and twenty we descry land but know not well in what height we be resolve that it be java but know not what part of it suppose it the southside and that we be fall on it by keep too easterly a course and though the plait make it to lie betwixt eleven and twelve degree and our latitude at that time be but eight degree forty minute yet it be questionable whether it have be discover but howsoever or wheresoever we be it be certain that we be fall to lee-ward of the strait of Sunda by two or three degree and into the northwest monsons which blow thereabouts from September to the last of March. all the master be of opinion to go back into thirteen or fourteen degree southward to fetch the southeast wind which be a trade wind between twenty eight and eleven degree and so to shape our course more northerly other be of opinion to go round about the island and to fetch Bantam as certain dutchman have do heretofore on like occasion and accomplish it in six week space but the first opinion take place the land hereabout be very high and near the sea full of great tree the air noisome by stink from the shore subject to much lightning thunder and rain with sudden gust the next day noon we have a good observation in the latitude of eight degree thirty five minute the general be resolve to beat up and down to see if we can get any thing to the west he charge m. Wilson for author of the error betwixt who also and the captain Wilson accuse as also for the loss of the Th^masine afterward strong current pass both word and blow which the general reduce into amity the eleven of january on the eighteen we have land in seven degree ten minute be by likelihood not far west from our first land notwithstanding that we have run from it by our course near one hundred league to the west by reason of a violent current to the east the land to the sea be low and level within high mountain we anchor at the entry of the bay where we find calm the current set strong east southeast that in a calm it will carry a ship four league a watch there be store of wood and water from the rock but brackish we find near to the shore continual calm the wind still blow two or three league off at sea be it never so great a storm in this place enforce Bay which I may well call enforce bay we see no people the shore very thick of wood palm and a hundred other kind of tree some grow in a number of root * * indian figtree or arbory (@) whic^ Co^op^us concede to be the tree of Adam sin see my Pilgr. l 5. c. 13. @. 2. which descend from the top of the branch which be forty or fifty foot high and take root again so that the tree show like a woodstacke I suppose that never Christian have be there nor will again if he can avoid it yet the general in one of the tree set up his name and arm we be not pass two league from our anchor place from whence we have scant wind enough to bring we but there rise so great a gust of wind and rain that we be force to take in all our topsail with diverse other intelligence IAnuary the four and twenty 1614 we set sail from Gravesend the second of February sir t. Ro^ sir Thomas roe ambassador from his majesty to the great mogoll repair aboard the lion with fifteen follower and master Humpherey boughton aboard the peppercorn recommend to the company by his majesty to pass into India we carry with we in the fleet eleven japoneza bring into England by the Clove divide proportionable among the ship likewise fourteen guzerats bring by the dragon also nineteen condemn person out of Newgate japonezes guzerats and condemn person to be leave for discovery of unknown place the company have obtain the king pardon for they to this purpose on the twenty some of the dragon man the newgate-bird among attempt to run away with their pinnace which then be prevent but one of those condemn with two of the pepper-corne company carry away her pinnace next night two of my ship company have conspire to carry away the boat but be discover the three and twenty we set sail out of the down on the six of march lose sight of the lizard and on the six and twenty have sight of land which we suppose the westermost part of Forteventura 1615. map false in cape Boyadore and Marpequena and prove part of Barbary one of the land point enter the river Marpequena be misgraduate one whole degree more northerly than it shall be likewise cape Boyadore be misgrade one degree as we then find by experience escape great danger cause by that error in our plait the six and twenty the general wind begin the ten of May be by reckon distant from the cape of good hope bear east a quarter south six hundred and twenty league we see many pintado Mangareludas and other fowl whereof I have not hear the like the five of ^une we anchor in the bay of Soldania have not bury above three or four in the whole fleet Soldania corey a savage which have be in England about thirty be now sick we build five tent corey come down and welcome we after his manner by who mean the people be nothing so fearful as at other time nor so thievish they bring we cattle in great abundance which we buy for copper shred corey show some of our people his house wife and child at a town thence distant five english mile contain about one hundred house most of they can say sir Thomas smith english ship which they often with great glory repeat their wife and child come often down to we to who we give great content with bugle and the like and two or three desire to go for England see corey have speed so well and return so rich with his copper suit which he yet keep in his house very chary corey also determine to return and to carry one of his son when our ship be thence find home-ward on the east-side of the table be another cottage of ten small house build round like bee-hive cover with mat make of bents weave together the sixteenth we set on shore by consultation ten condemn person to remain at the cape their house ten condemn person set on shore viz. John cross Henry Cocket clerk Brand bouth Hunnyard Brigs pet metcalfe Skilligall we give each man something for his own defence against wild beast and man weapon and victual they consent cross shall be their head the people desire brass and se^ not so much by copper they desire piece of a foot or more square iron hoop they care little for we catch seven or eight hundred fish in the river with and root cut away and the juice of the rest press out and boil to a certain height after put up in earthen pot stop close so stand eight month and last put in small skin to sell. the north part of the voyage to surat the five of june we anchor in the road of Soldania uncertainty of the variation though the variation be a excellent evidence in the whole course of veer land yet it deliver no other certainty but warning to look out for it lessen not in the same proportion near land but by a much slow for which I can give a perspicuous reason but too large for this place nor can any judgement at all be make to twenty league thereby that shall be infallible the magnetical amplitude be so difficult to observe true by the ship motion and the needle quickness that a degree be scarce a error this consideration make i confident that we shall see no land until the five day early in the morning Soldania be as I suppose a island in the south end whereof be the cape of good hope Soldania divide from the main by a deep bay on the southeast side and due east by a river which we discern upon the table the land be fruitful bear short thick grass the main be divide with most high and steep rocky mountain cover with snow and unaccessible except it be search by the river of which doubtless be very great fall into the bay on the east side there be on the island five or six hundred people the most barbarous in the world eat carrion wear the gut of sheep about their neck for health and rub their head curl like negro with dung of beast and dirt they have no other clothe then beast skin wrap on their shoulder the skin next the body in heat in cold the hairy side their house be but one mat concave like a oven into which they creep and turn they about as the wind change for they have no door to keep it out they have leave their steal by trade with we and by sign make show their heart be good they know no kind of God or religion the air and water be very good and wholesome and both of they subtle and search there be on the island bull cow Antelops baboon mole of great bigness feasant partridge lark wild-goose duck Passerflannugos and many other on Pengwyn there be a foul so call that go upright Pengwin island his wing without feather hang down like sleeve face with white they fly not but walk in path and keep their division and quarter orderly they be a strange fowl or rather a miscellaneous creature of beast bird and fish but most of bird confute that definition of man to be animal bipe implume which be near to a description of this creature the commodity here be first reasonable refresh with cattle so that a season be choose when they be not lean a month after the sun be depart from they northward Maugin root arras if our merchant be not a building accompany with about fifty man his apparel be a mantle of blue and red linen wrap about he to his knee his leg and foot bare on his head a close cap of chequer work the interpreter be certain magadoxian that speak arabic and break portuguese captain Newport present he with a piece and a sword blade from capt. keeling receive a welcome and command four bullock to be return in requital and with gravity enough entertain they give free liberty to buy and sell and signify so much by a messenger to the inhabitant round about and promise to send down his own cattle but profess he have no power to compel or make price for other but leave the trade open to every man will he send for Coco nut to give the company himself chew Bittle and lime of burn oyster-shel with a kernel of a nut call Arracca like a akorne it bite in the mouth avoid rheum cool the head strengthen the tooth and be all their physic it make one unused to it giddy and make a man spittle red and in time colour the tooth which be esteem a beauty this be use by all man hourly from the governor they be lead to a carpenter house a chief man of that town the house build of lime and stone plaster with wall town able to put out a thousand horse arm and as many shot a river to pass which a few man will defend against a good army give just occasion of scorn and offence and which the prince apprehend JAMES by the grace of almighty God the creator of heaven and earth king of great Britain France and Ireland defender of the christian faith etc. to the high and mighty monarch the great Mogor king of death THOMAS Coryate from the court of the great mogoll resident at the town of Asmere in the eastern India on Michaelmas day 1615. I do enjoy at this time as pancraticall and athletical a health as ever I do in my life and so have do ever since I come out of England save for three day in Constantinople where I have a ague which with a little let blood be clean banish the lord be humble thank for his gracious blessing of health that he have give unto i I be rob of my money both gold and silver but not all by reason of certain clandestine corner where it be place in a city call Diarbeck in Mesopotamia the turk country by a spahee as they call he that be one of the horseman of the great Turk but the occasion and circumstance of that misfortune will be too tedious to relate notwithstanding that loss I be not destitute of money I thank God since my arrival here there be send unto this king one of the rich present that I have hear to be send to any prince in all my life time it consist of diverse parcel one be elphant whereof there be one and thirty and of those two so glorious adorn as I never see the like nor shall see the like again while I live for they wear four chain about their body all of beat gold two chain about their leg of the same furniture for their buttock of pure gold two lion upon their head of the like gold the ornament of each amount to the value of almost eight thousand pound sterling and the whole present be worth ten of their leak as they call they a leak be ten thousand pound sterling the whole a hundred thousand pound sterling to the high seneschal of the right worshipful fraternity of sireniacall gentleman that meet the first Friday of every month at the sign of the meremaid in Bread-street in London give these from the court of the great mogoll resident at the town of Asmere in the eastern India right generous jovial and mercurial sirenaicke I have often read this greek proverb (@) (@) (@) (@) (@) that be one hand wash another and the latin this letter by m. god creator and saviour superstition and impiety most abominable in the high degree of these brutish ethnic that be alien from Christ and the commonwealth of Israel after I have see this show I will with all expedition repair to the city of twenty day journey from this and so into Persia by the help of my bless Christ etc. your dutiful love and obedient son now a desolate pilgrim in the world send he be good meat or no who reply he neither hear of nor see any hog whereat the king remember to who this hog be deliver cause the fellow to be send for and examine the matter have it confess how he throw away the hog and never carry it home the king press to know the reason the poor fellow answer how he be mock for touch it and it be a thing odious to the moor for shame he throw it away at which he reply by your law there be no difference of meat and be you ashamed of your law or to flatter the mahometans do you in outward thing forsake it now I see thou be neither good Christian nor good mahometan but a dissemble knave with both while I find thou sincere I give thou a pension which now I take from thou and for thy dissimulation do command thou to have a hundred stripe which be present give he in stead of his money and bid all man by his example take heed that see he give liberty to all religion that which they choose and profess they may stick unto I have think at first to have finish all these indian voyage in this four book but perceive it to grow into such greatness and withal such great alteration as the turkish trade at Moha and especial the persian at jasques have cause in the english trade with the contrary attempt of the portugal and chief the dutch before no good friend and there the worst of enemy to the english-indian trade I think fit to make thereof a Cranganor cast^e and island promise to the English and my successor after i to endeavour the take in of the fort of Cranganor and to possess the english thereof as their own with the island thereof which be in length on the sea-coast nine mile and in breadth three provide that I purpose to build therein a house for some of my own people to the number of one hundred person cochin promise and covenant to be give to the English I will also endeavour with the aid of the english hereafter to take in the fort and town of cochin belong former to my crown and kingdom and then to deliver it into the possession of the english as their own proper land and possession provide that the charge of the surprise be equal bear the one half by myself the other by the english nation and the benefit of the spoil thereof in whatsoever quality the one half to belong to i the other half to the english nation the Samorine to have no right title or interest in the aforesaid town precincts or appurtenance of cochin at all and the Samorine do also covenant for himself his heir and successor that the whole trade of the english in whatsoever commodity bring in or carry out shall pay yield or allow no manner of custom imposition tax toll or any other duty of whatsoever quality and to these covenant which the shortness of time do not permit to amplify I the Samorine have religious swear by the great
